en: Preface to the Record of Utmost Faith in the Pure Land As for this single Dharma of the Pure Land, it is like spring rain falling upon the earth and the bright sun shining in the sky: there is no root that it does not moisten, and no capacity that it does not illuminate.
Those who possess faith, practice, and vows will all attain rebirth; even those who are reckless men of the ten evils, when confronted with the signs of hell, [turn toward it].
Manifesting now, one may transcend horizontally through ten recitations at the moment of death. Were it not for the power of Amitābha’s sixteenth and eighteenth vows, who could achieve such a thing?
This may be called the most expedient means among all the sudden and perfect teachings. Master Lien-ken’s *Record of Utmost Faith in the Pure Land* specifically points to this principle;
he composed verses to praise it with all his might and analyzed the text of the *Amitābha Sūtra* in sequential order.

The sincere words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs provide a profound and earnest exposition. The phrasing therein is direct and straightforward, while its meaning is comprehensive and its principles profound.

Among all such verses and hymns, there is none that is not pertinent; they universally benefit both the wise and the ignorant, leading those who do not yet believe to find faith. This is precisely what is meant by the saying:
It is fully endowed with the three pillars of faith, practice, and aspiration; it completely cultivates the three trainings of scripture, reason, and discipline.
Every sentence unfolds from the resolve of what to adopt and what to abandon; every word flows forth from the mind of joy and aversion. Truly, it adds yet another raft to the ocean of suffering.
Having read it three or four times, I forgot both sleep and food; it was as if a great bell had startled me from a deep, ignorant slumber. Thus did it first arise.
I have slightly regained consciousness. It is as if a gale has blown away the thick, dark clouds, and gradually the light becomes visible.

Alas! I am of the lowest ignorance, blind and clumsy; my knowledge is shallow and my learning meager. To read this record is like a well-frog gazing at the vast ocean—I ultimately do not know what it is like.

I am ashamed that, being so clouded and dull-witted, I have obtained such benefit and yet only now begin to recover. How much more so would this be true for those who are talented, accomplished, and intelligent?
It has never happened that a person of wisdom, upon encountering this Dharma, failed to realize their own original nature and yet suddenly entered the Pure Land.
May those of like mind develop deep reverence and faith, truly uphold the Name, daily taking up what is good and discarding what is not, and hasten toward the Western Quarter.
Moment by moment rejoicing, moment by moment wearying, may we dwell together upon the jade lotus. Thus it is said.

Written on the sixth day of the summer month in the Ren-shen year of the Tongzhi era, by Jing Tai, a mountain man from Ruoyu, Hengjiang, prostrating himself at the Guanfo Lou (Hall for Contemplating the Buddha) in the hermitage of Longyan.

Preface by the Author:
The Buddha taught that human life is impermanent, briefer than a single breath. These two lines of admonition are truly a poignant wake-up call.
Yet, the body comes from karmic consciousness, and the mind departs with deluded thoughts. If one does not employ the single mind of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation) as right mindfulness...
Those who are clearly discerning know that at the moment of death, ten out of ten become deluded, like drifting dust tossed about by a turbulent wind, not knowing where it will be carried away.
How can those who possess Buddha-nature not stand in awe? Yet, the Buddha-dharma is like a vast ocean; one must rely on faith to enter it.

Among all the gates, the Pure Land is especially essential for faith. Prior to the arising of faith, there is no other wholesome dharma; once faith is established, one will certainly [attain liberation].
Again, I harbor doubts. This person truly believes in the Pure Land and practices genuine nianfo; they will certainly attain rebirth there in the future.

As for me, my ignorance is deep and my karmic burdens heavy; I am ashamed that not a single matter has been accomplished, and I possess not even a fraction of understanding. Fortunately, I have visited the four great sacred mountains and attended their teachings.
Each time, they pointed toward the great matter of birth and death, stating that among all methods, none is more direct and expedient than the single practice of nianfo.

It is indeed so. This is called being "thousandfold secure and ten-thousandfold certain," for one will surely arrive home. Apart from this single gate, there is no other dharma; it transcends all else.
Because it accords with my initial capacity, I joyfully prostrated and took refuge. I then proceeded before Amitābha Buddha, burned off a finger, and made this vow:
"From this moment until the end of the future, as long as my body exists, if my tongue does not rot, I shall hold the Name."

It does not cease. As long as the body does not die, one will not cease reciting the Buddha’s name. Since this is the vow, even if one should fall among the various classes of animals, there will still be no lack of a body or a tongue;
and possessing a body and a tongue, one will continue to recite the Buddha’s name without interruption.
Since the recitation of the Buddha’s name does not cease, even falling into such states is not a suffering. Why? Because one relies upon the power of the Buddha, like a prisoner who—

Since you are close to the presence of the King [Amitābha], what suffering could there be? Therefore, though my hindrances are as deep as this and my faculties as dull as this, I can only establish my vow in this manner;
for now, I shall simply believe with utmost faith, aspire with profound longing, and practice with steadfast devotion.
Out of reverence, I have composed thirty-two verses based on the text of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* and the words of the Buddhas and patriarchs, in accordance with the scripture.

This has been composed as a formal text; it is not the result of mere audacity. The subsequent forty-eight verses and other works have been compiled into a single volume titled *The Record of Utmost Faith in the Pure Land*.
Although these contain colloquialisms and coarse expressions, they do not deviate from the essential purpose of the Pure Land teachings.

Just as all streams flow toward the sea and ultimately converge in the taste of salt, so too does the sea flow into the streams—there is nothing that is either acceptable or unacceptable. Thus, though the writing may be crude and the language plain, the words [remain true to their intent].
Perhaps the wise, upon reviewing this work over time, will take pity on my lowly ignorance and recognize my earnest resolve.

I pray that you will calmly study its meaning, so that we may together believe in this gate and ascend together to the Land of Bliss. Do not reject these words because of the person who spoke them, thereby failing your own Buddha-nature;

for this record is specifically intended as a self-exhortation, compiled and recounted from what I have diligently practiced. How could I dare to present it for the public gaze? I am filled with trepidation.

How great! How deeply ashamed! *The Ritual for Reciting the Name of the Buddha and Reading Scriptures for Lifelong Upholding* The *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* states:
"Sentient beings of the ten directions who, with a sincere heart, believe and rejoice, desiring to be born in my land... and so forth.
"If ten recitations [of my name] do not arise [in his heart], may I not attain perfect enlightenment—except for those who commit the five heinous crimes or slander the true Dharma.

Furthermore, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: "Those who hear this sutra and uphold it, as well as those who hear the names of the various Buddhas, shall all be protected and remembered by all the Buddhas;
they shall all attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Thus we know that the three Pure Land sutras all possess inconceivable merit.

If even reciting the Buddha's name for as few as ten thoughts, or chanting the sutras, or merely hearing his name yields such results, how much more so for those who devote themselves wholeheartedly throughout their lives to faith and acceptance!
Therefore, from this moment forth, I make a vow regarding the fragrance of the precepts: I shall wholeheartedly uphold them and seek to attain the Pure Land.
Yet, these two characters "Pure Land" are truly not easy to reach. For those who have committed the five heinous crimes and the ten evil acts, when death approaches, the hells appear all at once;

yet even they can still be reborn there through ten recitations of the Buddha’s name, as attested in the sutras. How much more so for one who throughout the day upholds the sixty thousand great names? By means of this inferior [practice]...
This is superior. It is clearly evident that this is yet another manifestation of our Buddha’s extraordinary supreme compassion;
thus, among all skillful means, it opens up a most excellent one. In this way, even the lowliest of beggars may ascend to the precious realm.
How could even a body broken into pieces ever suffice to repay the Buddha’s grace? There is only the sincere and deep faith in holding the Name. Therefore, throughout the day...
Before the break of dawn, bowing one’s head toward the west, one completes the *Ciyun Shiqi Fo* (The Ten Breaths of Compassionate Clouds Buddha).
Thereafter, following the public liturgical procedures for recitation and practice, one reverently faces the Buddha before the western altar.

According to the ritual manual, one performs prostrations and visualizations, reciting the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* once and the *Wǎngshēng Zhòu* (Recitation for Rebirth) three times, followed by the hymn "Praise to the Golden-Colored Body of Amitābha Buddha," until reaching the phrase "Namo..."
Having prostrated three times toward the Western World of Ultimate Bliss to the Greatly Compassionate and Greatly Merciful Amitābha Buddha, rise and hold [the rosary].
Whether walking in circumambulation or sitting, proceed as you see fit. Recite until ten thousand recitations are reached for one session;

perform six such sessions, following the same format as the first. Upon completing sixty thousand recitations, perform the general dedication of merit. Then, kneeling, recite the name of Avalokiteśvara.

Śrī Avalokiteśvara and the assembly of the Pure Ocean, each having completed ten recitations, again contemplate the disciple’s recitation of the text for the Buddha-name of Amitābha, the Buddha of True Merit, up to the verse:
"May all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm together be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Next, conclude with the Three Refuges. As for the empowerment of the Forty-eight Vows of Amitābha Buddha, it is as follows: [The text continues with the specific verses of the Forty-eight Vows. ...is hereby concluded. May it be so.
According to one’s own physical strength: if one is capable, one should prostrate; if not, one should recite.

Once the ancestral patriarchs listed in the assembly of the Pure Land have been honored with bows, kneel again to recite the "Ten Breaths of Contemplating the Buddha," while also including Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and the assembly of the Pure Sea.
Each of these must also be recited ten times. Finally, recite once the "Text on Entering Contemplation at the Moment of Death" by Great Master Shandao. Regarding each of the above items:
This means that one’s practice of a single day’s Buddha-work remains unchanged until death and is maintained for a lifetime.

During this period, there may still be the performance of Pure Land repentance rituals and the recitation of the *Amitābha Sūtra*, which do not fall within the six fixed periods of daily practice; these must be undertaken through timely skillful means in order to make progress.
Even a slight lapse leads to accumulation—whether small or great. However, such practice is sustained throughout one's entire life; it is not the work of a single day.
It is like the constant flow of a small stream; its value lies in its being continuous and unceasing, rather than in ten instances of rushing force followed by one instance of stagnation.
Although the matter of birth and death should indeed be prepared for with urgency, even within that urgency there must be skillful means (*upāya*).

Those who do not yet comprehend this principle will inevitably suffer from a "tiger's head and a snake's tail," or else they will be possessed by demons—this is precisely what is meant. Is it not truly lamentable? I say: understand the meaning.

For those who practice with earnest devotion, it is sufficient simply to rejoice in the day and feel weary of it, severing all attachments, and never forgetting the single phrase "Amitābha Buddha" from moment to moment.
If one acts thus today, one will likewise act thus at the time of death.

With neither heat nor cold, passing away just as one went before, one will naturally possess a radiant countenance when reborn, returning safely to one’s native home; there is no need for the toil of pre-emptive anxiety. This is my lament.
With a heart filled with joy, I have here recounted this origin story to reveal the far-reaching nature of its pure causes. Thus it is said:
I praise the Buddha who took up this Sahā world as his teaching site— He whose supreme compassion fully reveals the rare and difficult-to-believe Dharma.
All Buddhas proclaim it widely and praise it together; the Compassionate Father of the Land of Bliss gathers us back to him.
All thousands of sutras point to this, which one should revere and trust; ten thousand sages alike return to the Terrace of Ultimate Bliss.
Only this Dharma-door is truly direct and swift; by hearing its name and holding it fast, one attains rebirth within the lotus womb.
Reflecting on oneself and abandoning the turbid path to death is a matter of great importance; this impermanence is truly tragic. Having lost this human body, it is indeed a cause for sorrow;
while the Great Matter remains unclarified, one truly cries out in anguish. Even when entering the three miserable realms, one must still feel profound and bitter distress.

Bound by the halter of passion and the chains of craving, one is self-entangled; like a silkworm spinning its own cocoon, one falls into the boiling cauldron—when will the mind of renunciation arise so that one may be liberated?
With sincere devotion, recite the Buddha’s name and aspire for the Western Land, giving rise to both joy in the pure and revulsion toward the impure.
In the cycle of birth and death, who can escape? Once the *kāṣāya* is lost, it is difficult to regain.
Dwelling temporarily in the dust of the world, one still falls into the three miserable realms; The retribution of suffering is hard to describe—only with trembling and sorrowful weeping.
All these causes arise from the three poisons; From this day forth, I repent deeply until they are daily eliminated.
With sincere devotion, I hold the Name and repent in my heart;
Vowing to be born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing, I shall personally behold the face of Amitābha Buddha. Only then will the deluded thoughts of my mind be satisfied;
having been born in that land for one lifetime and paid homage to the Buddha, I shall return to this Sahā world to propagate the glory of Sukhāvatī.
Not sparing body or life, I transform sentient beings; Exhorting all beings to return to the Pure Land.
Now, with joy and renunciation, I make this great vow: May the Buddha’s compassionate light receive me swiftly.
Having burned my finger, I make this vow to repent for my karma and aspire to seek the Western Paradise.
"Disciple, as for the fragrance of my precepts: from beginningless time until this present life, I have extensively committed the ten evil deeds and the five heinous crimes of immediate retribution;

all such transgressions are beyond the power of words to fully describe. Now that I have obtained a human body, greed, anger, and delusion abound; I have both committed these myself and incited others to do so."

Having seen and heard [these things], they rejoiced accordingly; yet in the future, they will certainly fall into the fiery pit. By these causes and conditions, they will constantly pass through the three miserable realms for hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas, with no time of escape for a long time.
Now, for the first time, they have attained awakening; they rend their hearts to confess and reveal [their sins], and call to mind the Buddhas of the ten directions.

He possesses great compassion and is able to rescue and deliver me and all sentient beings. If one’s remorse is not sincere or one’s resolve to uphold [the practice] is not earnest, it will be difficult to move the Sage.
Therefore, from beginning to end, I have made vows with a devoted heart and continued burning four fingers as a universal offering.
First, I extended three fingers in sincere devotion to offer to our original teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha, of this Sahā world.

And to all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time: may I swiftly abandon the suffering of this Sahā world and, until the end of the future, extensively deliver sentient beings so that they likewise abandon this suffering.
Again extending a single finger, I offer sincere devotion to Amitābha Buddha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss;
may I swiftly attain the bliss of the Western Paradise and, until the end of the future, extensively deliver sentient beings.
May all beings together partake of this merit. Though space may come to an end, my vow shall be inexhaustible.

Furthermore, having reverently burned incense from my arm over time, I entreat Amitābha Buddha to constantly come and provide protection, so that my disciples’ roots of goodness shall not be obscured and their pure causes shall increase.
When the time of death eventually arrives, may their bodies and minds be possessed of right mindfulness, their sight and hearing clear and distinct, and may they behold the Buddha face-to-face.
Amitābha Buddha, Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and the assembly of Bodhisattvas, holding flower pedestals in their hands, come to welcome and guide me.

In the space of a single thought-instant, I am born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Upon the blossoming of the lotus flower, I behold the Buddha and immediately hear the Buddha-vehicle, suddenly awakening to the Buddha-wisdom.

Above, for my parents of past kalpas and my deceased father and mother of this life; below, for all beings of the four modes of birth within the Dharma-realm, and for both the existent and non-existent states of mind—relying upon these...
This is the excellent cause for making this vow: may we swiftly ascend to the Pure Land and all attain rebirth there. Without withholding my earnest entreaty, I universally dedicate these merits.
By means of this causal power of the vow, may I adorn the Buddha’s Pure Land, and together with all sentient beings, be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

at the time when my life is about to end, Have all obstacles completely removed,

universally vowing that all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm may together be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
