In accordance with the sutras, I accept and believe this single phrase: "Namu Amida Butsu.
Spoken by the Compassionate One, the Teacher of this Sahā world, he has completely and utterly poured forth this difficult-to-believe Dharma.

"A single phrase of Amitābha Buddha—Śākyamuni’s earnest exhortation, 'Believe my words,' and that which has been spoken by all Buddhas: this dharma is difficult to believe and difficult to encounter—a single phrase of Amitābha Buddha.
The Buddhas of the six directions collectively extol it, extending their broad and long tongues to praise and encourage it."
A single phrase of Amitābha Buddha can be measured; he is protected and remembered by all Buddhas. Those who hear his name and uphold it are all *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive).
A single phrase of "Namu Amida Butsu": its radiance and lifespan are inconceivable; it universally gathers all who practice nien-fo, and their rebirth is without exception.
A single phrase of "Namu Amida Butsu": its merit and adornments are immeasurable; they are all formed of the four precious gems within the true lotus pond.

With one phrase of the auspicious sign, "Amitābha Buddha," he offered a profusion of exquisite flowers as an offering to the myriad Buddhas. Then, in the very space of a mealtime, he returned to his own land and entered it.
With one utterance of "Namu Amida Butsu," lotus flowers as large as chariot wheels bloom in the pond, their colors—blue, yellow, red, and white—beyond compare in this world.
With one utterance of "Namu Amida Butsu," there is no longer the experience of any suffering; all enjoy happiness, for those three evil realms do not exist. Therefore, it is so named.

The single phrase of the Nembutsu, "Amida Butsu," is the means by which you should now resolve to attain birth in the Pure Land. Why is this? Because it is the supreme and excellent path for all people.
A single invocation of "Namu Amida Butsu" cannot be achieved through meager roots of goodness; yet, by holding the name and being born in that land, it becomes a source of immense merit.
If one holds the name for seven days, reciting with a single mind without distraction, at the time of death, one will certainly—

Moved by a single phrase of the Buddha Amitābha, The profound and vast vows of Dharmākara— sixty-eight in number— If one’s ten recitations are uninterrupted, One shall attain rebirth even while still bearing karmic defilements.

A single phrase of "Namu Amitabha Buddha" has the most extensive affinity for those in this world of five turbidities; other gates are difficult to accomplish, whereas holding the name is the easiest way to go.
A single phrase of "Namu Amitabha Buddha" utterly extinguishes boundless sins and transgressions; it is like iron being used as ballast for a boat, ensuring that one will certainly not sink.

Immersed in the single phrase "Namo Amitābha Buddha," the Buddhas of the ten directions open the gates of skillful means, praising it with one voice in common accord; thus doubts are severed and faith is born.
A single phrase of "Namu Amitabha Buddha": the Tripitaka and the twelve divisions of the canon all point this out. You should know that this is a great causal condition;

one should practice mindfulness of the Buddha with fierce and earnest resolve. A single phrase of "Namu Amitabha Buddha": the vows of Samantabhadra in the Avatamsaka Sutra are most urgent, and the same applies to Mañjuśrī. One should maintain this [practice] without wavering.

Rest in the single phrase "Amitābha Buddha. This is the oral transmission handed down by the successive patriarchs of the Lotus Society. When the Buddha’s name enters a distracted mind, that very distracted mind is itself the Buddha.

A single phrase of "Namu Amida Butsu" is a most rare and difficult-to-believe Dharma. Like a single myrobalan fruit within the great trichiliocosm, how fortunate it is that this one phrase has been granted to my mouth!
It universally gathers all capacities through inconceivable means; those who believe, accept, and extol it shall all ascend to the stage of non-retrogression.

A single phrase of Amitābha Buddha for those retreating from the stages: even those flowing horizontally through the five realms of existence can completely transcend them. If success is achieved merely by hearing His name, how much more so when the sound does not cease?
The single phrase "Namu Amitābha Buddha" must rely upon both a sincere heart and earnest practice. This is the threefold tally and contract; by presenting this ticket, one will surely be gathered in.
The single phrase "Namu Amitābha Buddha"—the Unsurpassed King of Physicians—saves all from the myriad ailments of kalpas; if one can take it, one shall certainly be healed.

To extinguish [all afflictions] with a single phrase of "Namu Amida Butsu" is difficult to encounter even in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas. When a beggar obtains such a treasure, he possesses joy and is free from sorrow.
"A single phrase of Amitābha Buddha—how tragic that no one finds it easy to travel this path! Alas for me, the lotus root; my karma is heavy and my transgressions deep.

A single phrase of Amitābha Buddha is the compassionate vessel upon which to rely across the shoreless sea of suffering. I only pray that people will be willing to board it, so as to arrive safely at the ultimate destination."

The single phrase of the Land of Bliss: Amitābha Buddha, The Great Compassionate Father, in whom ten thousand virtues are perfectly integrated. I and all sentient beings alike, Vow to be swiftly reborn in the Pure Land.
One phrase of Amitābha Buddha—clear, vivid, and truly extraordinary. Contemplating the wondrous existence within true emptiness, the bottom of the lacquer bucket has long since been removed.

One phrase of Amitābha Buddha: neither existence nor non-existence is established; it is lively and vibrant. The three spheres are empty in their essence and pure; one personally pays homage to Amitābha.
"A single phrase of Amitābha Buddha—neither investigating nor awakening—is a good news. It is dense yet continuous; its vertical and horizontal flow is most carefree and elegant."
A single phrase of Amitābha Buddha— Vast, luminous, and unclouded, most intimate to the crown of the head; Stainless, pure, and free from increase or decrease, Its wondrousness is beyond description.
With utmost faith, I universally exhort all.
The Great Sage of the West is named Amitābha; With his golden arm, its topknot whorls, he reaches down with earnest care to guide us.
If one holds his name, one will certainly leave Saṃsāra;
To practice nianfo, one must rely on the depth of one’s vows and deeds. From dawn until dusk, one must be diligent and earnest.
One must know that as soon as the Buddha’s name is uttered, the lotuses in King Bimbisāra’s pond have already blossomed.
There is no peace within the three realms; truly, one should feel deep sorrow. In this glowing red house on fire, there is nowhere to flee.
Although the Western Land offers the path of horizontal transcendence, how can one attain birth there without reciting the name of Amitābha?
In other paths, the study of the Way is most difficult to accomplish; How many who are clever waste their efforts on the surface!
Though they plan for appearances, it does not aid the matter; Only at the moment of death do they regret—whom can they blame?
Even those of evil and rebellious nature, mere ordinary folk, can still easily be reborn; How much more so for those of pure goodness—why would they fail to ascend?
Simply rely on faith and aspiration to diligently recite the ten recitations; It is valued solely in the sincerity with which one person recites the Buddha’s name.
Do not mock the recitation of the Buddha as being like an old woman’s chant; This Dharma is perfectly penetrating and immeasurable.
Even Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī have made vows for it; The sages and saints of all times have praised it in unison.
Buddha-remembrance perfectly encompasses ten thousand capacities; In the teachings of the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Pure Land, all find refuge.
What difference is there between the wise and the foolish, the noble and the lowly? Is this Dharma strange or not?
Though birth in the Pure Land by "transverse transcendence" is easy, One must also have sincere faith and a truly earnest vow.
The most foolish and the most clumsy can all reach [enlightenment], Provided they are diligent and maintain a single-minded resolve.
I address the guests of the three teachings in this Sahā world: Believe and uphold the Buddha’s name without ceasing your voice.
This floating life is like a dream; there is little time to rest. In the blink of an eye, the occupants of a room have changed.
A single change of room inevitably brings confusion; the loss of the spiritual throne is truly a cause for grief.
To exchange a phoenix palace or dragon tower for a thatched hut—once that happens, one will cry out in despair, unable to find a way back.
Seize this illusory physical form while you may to cultivate well; hold fast to Amitābha and never let go.
Day and night, never leaving the Buddha; When merit is perfected, one enters securely the Land of Bliss.
If you ask what strategy is required for rebirth there:
One must rely on joy and aversion, take it seriously, And hold the Great Name with a single-minded heart. Even those of different species can thus attain rebirth.
Heavy karma is like a stone that must be carried by boat; Shallow roots are like a fly hitching a ride on a galloping horse.
When the Dharma and its metaphors converge upon infinite power, Why worry about failing to transcend the journey through mindfulness of the Buddha?
Amitābha Buddha has already made the arrangements; He will surely come to deliver all who are lost.
Gazing long toward the opening of the Kōji airway, I beat my breast and stamp my feet, wailing in grief.
The Buddha has preached boundless sūtras, His compassionate heart healing and rescuing the ailments of sentient beings.
If one reads the prescriptions but does not take the medicine, what use is it? Quickly swallow the divine elixir: the ancient Buddha.
Having clarified that the principles of management are not for ordinary people, The practice of *samatha* and *vipaśyanā* regarding Amitābha is most easily accomplished.
In accord with the Pure Land teachings, this is true *nianfo*; Relying on the sutras, one should properly seek the original root.
Building bridges, paving roads, and making offerings to the Sangha, Along with abstaining from killing and releasing living beings, are the foremost causes.
Furthermore, dedicate all merit through the recitation of the Name; With blessings full and wisdom complete, one will be reborn in the highest grade.
Though one has committed a thousand kinds of karma and sins reaching to the heavens, In an instant, one will surely be bound before the prison records.
The suffering of having the tongue pulled out and the intestines drawn forth while being sawn asunder— Quickly recite Amitābha’s name with a resolute and joyful mind.
Wondrous medicines cannot cure the truly fatal disease; Heterodox prescriptions and deviant arts poison the heart-mind.
For those whose lives are at stake, a swift purging is required; One must urgently call upon the Supreme Honored One, the King of Physicians.
Discern carefully between the fish eyes and the pearls; Among them are ninety-six heterodox paths.
Poisonous drugs abound, yet few possess true knowledge;
How many are deluded by greed, ignorant and blind, bringing ruin upon themselves and others—a sight most heartbreaking.
When death arrives and the wrathful Yama appears, Fearing the azure iron countenance of the underworld, Reform your ways, recite the Buddha’s name, and strive with diligent vigor.
Cultivation relies entirely upon virtuous teachers and friends; Without meeting such teachers and friends, how can one emerge?
To fabricate arbitrarily without the slightest sense of shame— How could one avoid anxiety at the moment of death?
If practicing Chan, one must certainly recite Amitābha’s name; If one recites Amitābha’s name, there is no need for Chan practice.
Pure Land without Chan is truly stable; Chan without Pure Land is merely thirteen rounds of triple-inquiry.
Chan and Buddha-recitation are fundamentally no different; In the suchness of Chan and Pure Land, one contemplates the Dharma King.
If you can personally behold Amitābha, What hindrance is there in the absence of Chan mechanisms?
Reciting the Buddha’s name is not difficult; it is the death-mind that is difficult. First purify the basket of miscellaneous goods;
only when all within it has been gathered up will you be in accord. Clearly discern Amitābha as the ultimate inquiry:
birth, old age, sickness, and death are but racing bubbles, Rising and falling waves that form empty spheres in the void.
A single gust of wild wind has scattered it all, Not a trace of its fine marks remains.
The convergence of the eight sufferings is truly pitiable; In health one creates karma, yet now one suffers the cold.
Who knows that one will depart naked and empty-handed? One regrets not having returned early to the Buddha-recitation altar.
It is most fitting to recite the Buddha’s name while in the prime of life; do not wait until old age when hands and feet are already frantic.
Seeing green grass already burying black hair, seize the moment to uphold the practice and await the lotus chamber.
When old, the light of life is piteously meager; unpredictable impermanence occurs in a single instant.
Urgently hold the Name with fierce resolve; Do not let yourself waste away for ten thousand kalpas.
Whenever you hear of illness, know it to be a wondrous remedy; This fleeting body shall not remain long.
Constantly and joyfully recite Amitābha’s name to return to the Land of Bliss; The lifespans there, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, cannot be measured.
When death approaches, do not be alarmed; Fix your mindfulness on Amitābha and face his direction.
Casting all affairs aside, focus on that single thought; The Guide will surely board the compassionate vessel for you.
Though the poor and lowly toil in hardship all day long, It is only because of hunger and cold that their mouths are deprived of food.
Is it not better to be diligent in reciting the Buddha’s name? In other realms, food and clothing are naturally abundant;
do not boast of being a person of pleasure. From of old, virtue has been honored while gold and silver have been held cheap;
Only those on the superior lotus throne are truly noble, And only the wealth of one's own nature is reckoned as true.
If you urge an old man to practice *nienfo*, he says, "Wait for the sky to clear; let us do it next year.
Who knows if he will die before his leisure ends? Do not regret it; do not steal moments from your busy life.
Though practicing *nienfo* in leisure may seem relaxed and easygoing, impermanence is swift and leaves not a single moment behind.
Prepare your provisions and gear in advance, so as to avoid the burden of anxiety at the last moment;
reflecting on this from beginning to end is truly pitiable. I fervently entreat the Great Compassionate Old Immortal:
if you wish to depart from Saṃsāra, there is no other method than to hold fast to the Great Name with a resolute mind.
How tragic, how painful—this body of mine! Distracted thoughts fly about, with nothing ever accomplished.
Relying on the compassionate power of Amitābha’s vows, Even ten recitations performed morning and evening can lead to rebirth in the Pure Land.
Shaving the head and donning the dyed robes is for the sake of a profound cause; Yet all say they do so only to prostrate and repent for the sake of delivering deceased spirits.
I ask: has the repentance for one's own nature been accomplished? If not, you must urgently and diligently recite the Buddha’s name.
A hundred years of time is but a single kṣaṇa; Amidst leisure, busyness, and toil, suffering abounds.
Knowing that death arrives with empty hands, Quickly and single-mindedly take up the recitation of the Buddha.
The lost child has been away from home for fifty years; In delusion he created karma, his sins filling the heavens.
From this day forth, first awakened, he bares his heart; Daily he holds the Great Name sixty thousand times.
The Buddha’s compassionate vows are truly immeasurable; They dry up the black waters of beginningless samsara.
As mist disperses and clouds clear, the red sun appears; The accumulated karma of years is transformed into refreshing clarity.
Arising and ceasing originally stem from a single thought; Abandoning the root to pursue the branches, consciousness soars aloft.
If one recognizes the path to the source within this, Through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, Amitābha is that which is false and yet true.
In the breaths of birth and death, there is no room for sentiment; Hasten to prepare your provisions and await the journey.
This is not merely a brushstroke of talk about death; These are words of true feeling, not a fraction off the mark.
I prostrate to the Great Teacher of Peaceful Nurturing; With compassion, please take me, a fool, under your care.
Having suffered through many lifetimes, one now finally awakens; One makes a vow:
"The Jade Pond of Deluded Thought is truly excellent, with its fragrant flowers.
This is precisely when one’s mindfulness of the Buddha is powerful, pure, and singularly refined—do not let it slip away! At this moment, contemplating the Buddha is wondrous and immeasurable.
I am ashamed that my past karma has brought me to this Sahā world; Fifty years of time have passed in a single instant.
Neither a layman nor a monk, I am ashamed to remain within the lotus bud.
Why do I wear the shaven head? Having nothing of substance, I grow weary of this Sahā world.
Stoically holding to one phrase of Amitābha Buddha, Foolishly imagining the West as a nest for seeking joy;
With pen in hand, I speak flowery words of unsettled meaning— Do not mock, do not laugh, but examine with quiet discernment.
I dare not present this clumsy work as a masterpiece, But with earnest resolve, I offer these rough verses to encourage the cause of purity.
Cease human passions;
like mountain streams and moon reflections, life is hard to retain. Vigilantly guard yourself at every moment lest you fall into the Nine Dark Realms.
O noble guests who come and go, do not cast your glances back; Bind these six great characters to the heart.
Impermanence is unfathomable; one knows not when it will arrive. Hasten your mindfulness of Amitābha and sit awaiting his arrival.
I inform you all: do not take me to task, For the days are pressing and life is hastening toward its end.
Please grant me leave for my daily recitations.
Sixty thousand times the Amitābha Sūtra recited six times; day and night, through the six periods, without ceasing for a moment.
Birth and death are unpredictable within a single breath; the outgoing breath is as difficult to expect as the incoming breath remaining.
In an instant, once the thread of life is severed, one is said to have transmigrated to another life.
Because of this, the Buddha limited the number of recitations; Rarely having even a moment’s leisure, I encountered a guest and caught a cold.
Suddenly chilled, then suddenly feverish, like being cast into a frying pan, My entire body boils with burning pain—what can be done?
The four great elements are originally suffering; how could one distinguish between the noble and the poor?
Only now do I realize the urgency of mindfulness of the Buddha, lamenting before the Ancient Buddha, King of Emptiness.
I pray only that the physical environment of this Sahā world may be shortened, so that I may swiftly dwell within the white lotus groves of the Land of Bliss.
Afflicted by illness, I weep for my parents;
my longing for them is so intense it is truly heart-wrenching. The wind-whipped trees wail in grief, a pain that breaks the heart;
there is no way to repay their boundless kindness. There is a text worthy of being used to strike upon the Great King of Physicians.
With a sincere heart, I uphold the name of Amitābha Buddha; I pray that you grant your compassion by universally radiating light, And with golden arms, personally and earnestly guide me across;
May my parents be quickly comforted as they ascend to the Western Land, There to make offerings to the Buddhas and dedicate merit to their ancestors. (Also used to admonish those who harbor doubts.)
I continue to offer to the Buddha by burning my four fingers; people mock me and laugh at me as if I were mad.
How could they know the profound and subtle mystery of the True Path? How could they understand that steadfast practice is the most supreme condition?
For the sake of the Dharma, I burn my body to seek the precious verses; seeking the profound mystery, I burn my arm to pay homage to the Golden Immortal.
Since the former sages have already done so, I shall follow their example; To repay my parents' kindness, I enter the precious lotus,
Yet I am unworthy to occupy the monks’ latrine—
asking myself why I have become a shaven-headed one, Ignorant and deluded, like one of the lowest sort.
Failing to achieve anything else, I have studied the Buddha’s teachings; With deluded thoughts, I cross over suffering by relying on the boat of compassion.
Amitābha originally welcomes those who recite his name; How could he fail to receive even those with evil lotus-roots?
I hope daily for a swift return to An-yang (Sukhāvatī); I vow to enter the ranks of the lower grade as soon as possible.
Nianfo (Buddha-recitation):
An Expression of My Feelings Having returned to the valley, I have long not stepped through my thatched door. I have severed all ties with the mundane world of right and wrong.
Sixty thousand recitations of Amitābha are my fixed daily practice; Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, I am never apart from it.
The sound of the mountain stream is truly like the broad and long tongue; Every bird in the mountains is none other than reciting Amitābha.
If one can realize the pure and void meaning within this, Why labor at contrived practices to realize Bodhi?
Cease all seeking and questioning.
Wandering through the south, north, west, and east, I visited famous mountains and ancient monasteries. (In the winter of the Jiǎzǐ year, I went up to Wǔtái in the north;
returning via Éshān, it was already spring of the Yǐgēnwǔ year. The profound gates of Confucianism and Buddhism are originally like this;
Only now do I realize that my sandals and copper coins were spent in vain.
I have traveled across myriad mountain paths, Exhausting my heart's source through wind and frost;
Now I lay down the face given by my mother— (To seek out the mystery of life and death everywhere, none is as supreme as the recitation of the Buddha’s name.
I hold fast to Amitābha without counting the years— (Only when death arrives shall I cease.)

Recalling the Buddha, the *Balanen jing* (Sutra on the Immeasurable Life), in the chapter on the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta’s mindfulness of the Buddha, says: "Suppose there are two people: one who single-mindedly remembers another, and one who single-mindedly forgets that person.
These two may meet or not meet throughout their successive lives; they remain as distinct as their physical forms."
The shadow does not deviate from the object. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions cherish sentient beings as a mother remembers her child.

If the child runs away, what can the mother’s remembrance accomplish? But if the child remembers the mother, then just as the mother remembers the child, the mother and child will not be separated throughout successive lifetimes.
If the minds of sentient beings remember the Buddha and recite the Buddha's name, they will certainly see the Buddha in the present and in the future; they shall never be far from the Buddha.

Far removed [from the need for effort], one does not rely on expedient means but attains the opening of the mind spontaneously. It is like a person who has been perfumed with incense; their body carries the fragrance. Alas!

This metaphor clearly transcends the sun and moon, reaching the ultimate limit without remainder. I am ashamed of my own deep obstructions of affliction, whereby my path of practice is difficult to accomplish.

Although I know that the Pure Land is the most supreme expedient—where even an ordinary person of evil and rebellious nature can be reborn through ten recitations of the Buddha’s name—I, [whose only fragrance is that of the precepts]...

One’s past karma is heavy; when reciting the Buddha's name, one falls into dullness and distraction. It is like being in the River Vaitaraṇī: even if one circumambulates with a harsh voice, it is difficult to achieve resonance.
How shameful and how tragic! Yet we rely on Amitābha, who possesses the vow to welcome those with ten recitations to rebirth in the Pure Land, encompassing all nine grades.
Therefore, it does not matter whether the mind is settled or distracted; one need only worry about forgetting.

This is what the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* means when it says that "even a single invocation of 'Namo Buddha' leads all together to the path of Buddhahood. Since the Buddha possesses such compassion and skillful means, it is simply a matter of maintaining constant mindfulness and never forgetting the Buddha’s name.
It is just like a mother who naturally longs for her child: if the child remembers the mother, why worry about her?

Am I not failing my children? Therefore, with sincerity and faith, I practice with diligence, never daring to slacken even slightly. Even if a thousand horses and ten thousand oxen were harnessed together, they could not pull back this resolve of mine.

Thus, I have respectfully excerpted passages from the scriptures and inscribed them upon the title board, naming it "The Dwelling for Recollecting the Buddha," and have further composed verses to record this.
If you wish to abandon the sufferings of Sahā, there is no other door for seeking protection than the Dharma of skillful means.
Nothing is more wondrous than mindfulness of Amitābha. Scatter your thoughts toward the source and maintain constant recollection; as each thought arises, the ocean of karma will dry up.
When your mindfulness reaches the stage of single-minded focus, resolve to take birth within the lotus calyx.
In my leisure from meditation, I have spontaneously composed these lines:
Pitiable is this one suffering monk, Long fallen into the mud, unable to emerge from the dust and grime.
Wild waves of thought toss him without constancy; Discursive thoughts fly about, closing off his heart-sutra.
Only when a bright pearl is cast in does the turbidity begin to clear; Only by reciting the Buddha’s name can one emerge from the root of suffering.
When the root is withered through such recitation, one sheds the lotus stalk; Magnificently and alone revealed, one is reborn facing the West.
Impermanence urges on with ever-increasing haste; It drives this mountain monk to return home.
The Sahā world of the five turbidities is truly a perilous realm; In the pure land of the lotus root, one joyfully plants their seeds.
When long awaited by superior friends gathered like clouds, Aśvaghosha and Avalokiteśvara accompany the Buddha as he swiftly arrives at the assembly place in the Land of Bliss.
There, one takes refuge beneath the flowers, transcending the womb-birth.
A Text for Returning the Mind to Nembutsu upon Awakening from a Dream:
The light of mountain streams and the reflections of the moon are illusory forms, lacking solidity; the resonance of bamboo and the sound of pines are empty echoes, devoid of reality.

Yet, the accumulation of arising and ceasing builds up like Mount Sumeru, and birth and death flow perpetually through the sea of suffering. Since beginningless time, though we have indulged in greed and anger...
Through delusion, one creates various evil karmas. If the physical forms of the karmas thus created were to exist, they could not be contained even within the entirety of the realm of empty space.
For this reason, one undergoes the evil realms with no prospect of escape—why is this so?
It is because our present single thought of delusion leads us to suffer boundless misery for ten thousand kalpas; yet, though deluded for long, if one is willing to awaken...
A person who dreams of undergoing punishment feels pain, yet upon waking, it vanishes. It is also like a merchant traveling east for many years who, in an instant, remembers he is still in the west;
without moving his feet, he turns his head and is instantly in the west. If a lost person is willing to awaken, it is likewise so.

This is what Master Ciyun meant by being born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss in the space of a single thought-moment. What is essential is dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*) and the recitation of the Buddha’s name.

It depends solely on whether one’s heart is earnest or not. How much more so for Amitābha Buddha, who once made forty-eight vows, each vowing to deliver sentient beings—even those who are reckless evildoers of the ten non-virtues—so that they may attain rebirth through ten recitations at the moment of death. One must understand the nature of these ten evils and the ten recitations.

If even those who are still thus can attain deliverance, how much more so for one who possesses the precepts, meditative concentration, and sincerity, and who throughout their life maintains the mindfulness of the Buddha through the three essentials of faith, practice, and aspiration?
To compare the inferior with the superior, and to examine the good against the evil, the distinction between them is clearly evident.

One need only lament that one cannot hold fast with earnest sincerity; once one holds fast with earnest sincerity, one must further fear a lack of single-mindedness. Once one is single-minded, [the goal is attained].

Furthermore, one fears that this state may not endure long. However, if one can maintain it with single-mindedness, unify the mind, and sustain that unity for a long time—continuing without interruption until death without changing—one will certainly attain rebirth.
If, despite being truly thus, one were still not to attain rebirth, [then the teachings would be false].
If it were so, then Amitābha Buddha and all the Buddhas of the ten directions would be guilty of falsehood.
Let us ask a sincere and upright gentleman: even he would have no differing words; how much less could the golden mouth of the God among Gods personally proclaim this and yet deceive me alone?
Therefore, such a thing is absolutely impossible; do not trouble yourself with hesitation. Rather, uphold the Name and maintain single-mindedness without distraction; this is the way of Amitābha.
This is the fundamental principle of the sutra and the warrant for rebirth in the Pure Land. Within it lies nothing less than the truly difficult-to-believe Dharma and rare events.
For those who seek to swiftly depart from the ocean of suffering and fly to be born in the Land of Bliss, there is nothing that surpasses these two lines at the crown of the head.
Alas! In this degenerate age, those of us whose precepts have lost their fragrance are foolish, inferior, and have long been submerged in the depths of samsara.
Thus, mired in delusion and ignorance, although I have outwardly mingled with the monastic community, I remain utterly bewildered; I have been unable to be moistened by the Buddha-dharma.
As summer passes and winter comes, I have not realized that my life has already reached the age of sixty. Since the days gone by are many, the days yet to come must be few.
Suddenly, impermanence arrives like a misty rain on a dark night; the path ahead is shrouded in blackness, while the road behind is filled with sorrow—how painful!
To cry out in vain is futile; there is no way to turn back. One must know that one is bare-chested and exposed, solitary and alone.

Since the desire for life cannot be fulfilled, it seems that even the desire for death cannot be attained—how can one bear this? Be cautious in solitude and reflect upon it; who would not be pained by heart?
Therefore, I am truly and sincerely distressed. How could I not be filled with foreboding dread and give rise to sorrow and fear?

If it were not for the compassionate vow of Amitābha to provide succor, and for those who have made the resolve to recite the Buddha’s name with such earnestness, it would be exceedingly difficult to transcend [this world].
My own karma is so heavy; how fortunate that I have encountered this Dharma-door of Buddha-recitation!

Now that I have received the power of the Buddha, I shall uphold it throughout my remaining life and vow never to be negligent, so as to prepare for the unforeseen. As the *Śāsana-parivarta Sūtra* says: "To restrain..."
"In one place: what matter is not resolved? I say that "to regulate" means to regulate the holding of the Name.

"In one place" means to unify the single mind so it is not distracted. "What matter is not resolved" refers to abandoning this Saha world and taking up the Land of Ultimate Bliss, even unto the realization of the fruit;
all this does not go beyond these eight characters of the sutra, and thus is accomplished in a single lifetime. Thus it was left behind.
If one teaches in accordance with Amitābha, then the two sutras will harmonize, and there will be nothing that does not fulfill one's intent. Alas!

Śākyamuni, the Compassionate Father, in his final discourse of supreme compassion, out of pity for the sentient beings of the末劫 (final kalpa) who have no door by which to enter, has preemptively bestowed his grace through skillful means and direct pointing.
If we speak of it in relation to myself, it was precisely for my sake that he compassionately revealed it; yet if we speak of it in relation to...
As for human beings, they are led by all living beings. Thus we know that it is not only those of middling or inferior capacity who must urgently practice the recollection of the Buddha (nien-fo);

even the sages and worthies of the highest rank have all attained realization through the recollection of the Buddha. This is because the Buddhas of the ten directions all became Buddhas by recollecting the Buddha;
there is scriptural evidence for this. It is like an examination official in the Confucian tradition who, without having studied the classics himself, is able to preside over the examinations.

Consider this, O Grand Minister! Therefore, know that even if one does not believe in the practice of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation) but instead performs various miscellaneous good deeds, though their merit may exceed Mount Sumeru, they still cannot attain birth [in the Pure Land].
How much more so for those who seek the Way through other gates—like an ant climbing a mountain, where ten thousand will not find success in one.
To practice *nien-fo* is like sailing with a full sail down a river; ten thousand practices lead to ten thousand arrivals. Moreover, the compassionate vows of Amitābha are vast and boundless.
The capacity [of the mind] does not grasp [them]. It is like the ocean, which receives the hundred rivers; it gathers both the pure and the defiled together.
Even so, I alone am ashamed that my mindfulness cannot be unified and my attachment cannot be lightened.

If, indeed, one discards everything except for the three robes, the water bottle, and the alms bowl—the requisites of practice—and regards nothing as anything other than light, lightening it until there is nothing left to lighten, then the mind of nien-fo (buddha-recollection) will surely become unified.
If one sincerely abandons all else and holds fast to the Name, there is nothing to be mindful of other than the Buddha; mindfulness is not divided.

When it is unified, and unified again, until there is no place where it is not unified, then thoughts of worldly affection will surely grow light. Once affection is light, mindfulness will surely become unified.

Once mindfulness is unified, the Buddha will surely become singular. When the Buddha is singular and mindfulness is unified, and mindfulness is unified upon the singular Buddha, then there is no Buddha outside the mind—only the Buddha.

Externally there is no mind; the mind and the Buddha are one and the same. As the moon appears upon a thousand rivers, the time for the fulfillment of the reward has arrived—without excess and without deficiency.

When right mindfulness is clear and distinct, the Three Sages appear simultaneously. By following the Buddha to be reborn in the Pure Land, one will finally realize its spiritual efficacy. With this humble sincerity, I dedicate my life and mind to going to An-yang (Sukhāvatī) for one lifetime.
Then, returning to the dusty streets of the mundane world, I shall manifest billions of bodies to exhort and guide the masses of deluded beings, so that they may likewise [attain liberation].
To emerge from the wheel of suffering and dwell together with the Buddha—having established this vow, what more need be said? (What more need be said? May it be as vast as empty space.)
The Verse for the Fifth Watch Patrol:
At the first watch of the night, report this to those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha: "Today’s worldly affairs are finished;
I have set upright the beam of my backbone and opened the Great Prajñāpāramitā. Quickly practice mindfulness of the Buddha! Today, too, has passed."

At the second watch, arrive quickly; cast away drowsiness and prostrate yourself. Once awakened, listen to me speak: Within the great dream of human life, one should cast away and harmonize distracting thoughts.
Quickly recite the Buddha’s name; do not wait for impermanence to strike at the third watch.
Birth, death, and impermanence are suffering. Since you have become a monk, you must awaken early; you need not serve the king’s commands. Do not...
Sweep the graves of your parents; quickly recite the Buddha’s name. Do not let the Four Watches of the Night arrive before you see King Yama.
Tell this to those who know how to recite the Buddha’s name: birth is most difficult, while death is easy.
How many clever people pass their lives in vain, unable to discern the true flavor! Quickly recite the Buddha’s name; impermanence arrives in an instant.
The fifth watch has ended. How can this great matter be resolved? My mindfulness is not unified; my years are already old. Amitābha is originally manifest before me—how many people have missed this!
Quickly recite the Buddha’s name! Reciting the Buddha’s name is the path to Buddhahood.
As for the "wandering inspector": he wanders among those who are heedless and inspects them regarding birth and death. In ancient times, people used a round log as a pillow.
This refers to the principle that one’s body does not even touch its bed or chair; yet people today are not so.
By day their various thoughts fly about like birds, and by night they are shrouded in a drowsy stupor. Consequently, at the moment of parting from birth and death, they have no connection whatsoever.
Thus, when they arrive before me, they cannot even utter the Buddha’s name in response; this is precisely the state of being in a deluded sleep.
It has come to this! How bitter, how lamentable! This fragrance of my precepts has made me what I am—a shaven-headed one.
There is every possibility that I shall fall into the three miserable realms; even hell will be difficult to escape. I entreat you, all you noble ones:
reprove me with compassion, pity me and urge me on with strict admonition. Do not mock me for following my example; quickly and with urgency, recite the Buddha’s name. Come at once to deliver me!
A Song of Exhortation to Recite the Buddha’s Name with Urgency:
On This Matter, My Heart Aches. It is truly a cause for sorrow; yet since sorrow is of no avail, one should simply recite the Buddha’s name.
My eyes weep until they swell; it is truly a cause for grief; yet since grief is of no avail, one should simply recite the Buddha’s name.
To be a person for a brief moment while constantly confined in the cage of hell is truly a cause for sorrow; yet since sorrow is of no benefit, it is better to practice the mindfulness of the Buddha.
Though one be a monk, if he is the same as the laity, it is truly a cause for shame; yet since shame is of no benefit, it is better to practice the mindfulness of the Buddha.
If one’s school is not clear and the teachings are not mastered, it is truly a cause for remorse; yet since remorse is of no benefit, it is better to practice the mindfulness of the Buddha.
My conduct lacks precepts, yet the three poisons are heavy; truly this is shameful, yet shame brings no benefit—recite the Buddha’s name!
I am fond of committing many sins, which will deliver me to the three miserable realms; truly this is terrifying, yet fear brings no benefit—recite the Buddha’s name!
I am fond of evil karma, which entangles me; pestilence and disease are fierce and truly fearsome, yet dread brings no benefit—recite the Buddha’s name!
The eyes grow dim and blind; The ears lose their hearing. Truly distressing! Since this distress is of no avail, It is better to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, even if the whole body burns.
The entire body aches with pain; Truly pitiable! Since this pity is of no avail, It is better to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, even when impermanence arrives.
Reaching out to touch empty space; Truly frantic! Since this franticness is of no avail, It is better to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
The various ghost-soldiers—terrible beyond endurance; truly pitiable. Since this misery brings no benefit, recite the Buddha’s name.
Your tongue is too large; your mouth is hard to move; truly distressing. Since this distress brings no benefit, recite the Buddha’s name.
The appearance of hell is excellent; the fires are uniformly red; truly terrifying. Since this terror brings no benefit, recite the Buddha’s name.
Fortunate to associate with virtuous friends; The mindfulness of the Buddha is deep—truly joyful, yet joy alone is of no benefit.
To practice mindfulness of the Buddha is to rely on the Buddha’s power; One obtains a cooling breeze—truly joyful, yet joy alone is of no benefit.

To practice mindfulness of the Buddha is for the mind to become somewhat clear; When focused mindfulness penetrates through—truly joyful, yet joy alone is of no benefit. To practice mindfulness of the Buddha is good.
Before the ten recitations are finished, the image becomes relaxed; this is truly cause for joy. Yet even this joy is of no benefit. It would be better to contemplate the forms of hell;
there is absolutely no trace of them. This is truly cause for joy. Since this joy is indeed beneficial, it is better to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.

It is good to rely upon spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) who assist in demonstrating one's merit. This is truly cause for joy. Since this joy is indeed beneficial, it is better to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
The manifested Buddha arrives, surrounded by lotus pedestals—truly joyful!

Since this joy is beneficial, it is good to practice mindfulness of the Buddha; like the sun, it is vast and great—truly joyful! Since this joy is beneficial, it is good to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.

It is good to dwell before others while practicing mindfulness of the Buddha; furthermore, one’s mind becomes sharp and clear—truly joyful! Since this joy is beneficial, it is good to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
In a single thought-moment, one shares in the Land of Bliss; truly it is a joy. Since this joy is beneficial, one should recite the Buddha’s name—how excellent is the recitation of the Buddha’s name!

How excellent is the recitation of the Buddha’s name! How excellent is the recitation of the Buddha’s name! Upholding the precepts and reciting the Name—how excellent! Regarding the various matters of peril mentioned above:

It relies entirely on the single phrase of the Buddha’s power for protection; one need not fear kings, nobles, or iron-hearted men. At the moment of death, returning to the source by reciting the Buddha's name is best.
This song was truly composed by my own hand as a sincere confession and a bitter, piteous exhortation to those who do good.
O person, you must believe with utmost sincerity that the practice of Buddha-recitation is of vital importance. As a great man, you should attend to this as your foremost and most urgent task;
do not treat it lightly out of self-importance. You must recognize that my "fragrance of precepts" is the result of having committed various evil karmas in the past and present.
At the moment of death, the various fires of hell will manifest all at once in this manner.

Yet, by relying solely on the merit of others’ assistance in reciting the Buddha’s name and the power of one’s own intense mindfulness, one may return from hell before even ten recitations have been completed, surrounded by lotus flowers.

Furthermore, one will be moved by Amitābha Buddha, who sends transformation Buddhas to console me; in an instant, I shall be gathered and transported to dwell together in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. How much more so for those who have performed many virtuous deeds!
To uphold the name through precepts and meditative concentration with such earnestness is the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha for a lifetime.
One must know that mindfulness of the Buddha possesses such excellent qualities, such advantages, and such spiritual efficacy; and that Amitābha Buddha possesses such compassion.
He is like parents to a thief: they never despise their child for being a thief, nor do they cease to love him. They will surely...
I must drag you back home. For such a grace as this, how could grinding one's bones to dust ever suffice as recompense?
Therefore, to again lack faith and again fail to keep [the teachings] in mind would be truly the utmost pity.

As for what is called "thorough awakening," how could one know this principle without reading the Buddhist scriptures or hearing the instructions? From this day forward, there is only the need to exert all effort in diligent cultivation.
Exhausting my remaining life, I return in sincerity; I shall do nothing but entrust my life to the recitation of the Buddha’s name. What more need be said?
A Verse of Prostration, Vows, and Dedication:
I prostrate to Śākyamuni, To Amitābha Tathāgata, And to all Buddhas of the ten directions.
The Sūtra of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, The Bodhisattvas, the Superior and Virtuous Ones,
And the Brahmā-like sages of Mount Lu— These ancestral patriarchs of the Lotus Society, Have reverently compiled the words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs To praise the Pure Land in verse.
I, this disciple, relying on the Buddha’s power, Uphold them with my head and accept them with constant faith.
I prostrate and pray that you will grant your protection, Speedily causing us to leave this Sahā world.
May all virtuous people who see or hear this Exhort one another in succession; Their virtue is immeasurable, And metaphors cannot fully express it.
I vow to dedicate this merit To the Buddha’s Pure Land, For myself and all sentient beings alike.
This record is for those who together aspire to the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
It is recorded that the fragrance of the precepts arises from within oneself; one must reflect deeply upon the fact that the matter of death is of great significance.

One must urgently and with all haste recite the Buddha’s name. If, during one's daily life, one has possessed even ten parts of true integrity, then in the future one will have at least a fraction of resistance against the obstacles of death.
Perhaps one may temporarily act as its master; otherwise, it would be a mere empty title that accomplishes nothing at all.
Therefore, the compiler has compiled this solely for self-exhortation, as a passport and guide for protecting oneself. How could I dare presume my abilities to represent others?
Now, to the west of Anqiang, there are virtuous gentlemen such as Xu Miaoming and others who have profound faith in the Western Pure Land; having seen this record...
He rejoiced at this beyond measure and requested, again and again, that it be carved into woodblocks for the benefit of the masses. I told him, "It cannot be. Why?
Because the text was composed by me based on the Buddha whom I could recall; it is truly not in accord [with the original], and the phrasing is coarse and crude.
Why should I take the trouble to invite much ridicule? He replied to me, saying, "Though what you say is true, Master," [he continued].
Yet, is it not difficult to present this to those of superior or middling capacity? Nevertheless, its shattering of our worldly sentiments is precisely appropriate for the occasion.
Why indulge in such excessive humility? It is like the instruction of a young scholar to a child; in the end, it can be mastered through self-study and will benefit others.
Why am I so afraid of being ridiculed? Reflecting back upon my firm refusal, since it was not granted, how could I dare persist in stinginess to cause others to withdraw their intentions?
For this reason, I have filled [the space] with a blush of shame; I am terrified, truly terrified. I prostrate myself and beseech you, my noble and virtuous friend:
out of compassion for my ignorance, please do not take this into account—it would be most fortunate. This is my earnest prayer.

In the spring of the Ren-shen year of the Tongzhi era, the student of Pure Practice, Liangen Jiexiang, bows his head and respectfully submits this "Text on Loathing and Departing from the Turbid World and Thinking of Returning to the Pure Land.
As for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, it says: "The three realms have no peace; they are like a burning house, filled with manifold sufferings, and are most truly terrifying."
"Fearful! Truly, these words are so. Within the realm of form, the realm of desire, and the formless realm, all sufferings and afflictions prevail;

there is no peace or security whatsoever. Only within the Pure Land of the West are all terrors severed, afflictions utterly eliminated, and even the names of various sufferings do not exist, for one experiences only bliss.
Therefore, it is named 'Ultimate Bliss' (Sukhāvatī). Furthermore, the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* says: 'If one calls upon my [name]...'"
One will certainly be born in my land. If this were not so, I would vow never to attain Buddhahood. The *Lotus Sūtra* further states:

"If a person, even with a distracted mind, enters a stupa or temple and once calls out 'Namo Buddha,' they shall all together attain the path of Buddhahood. Alas! A thousand scriptures point in the same direction, and ten thousand sages proclaim it in unison.
If one does not believe the words of the Buddha, what words can be believed? One must know that by calling upon the Buddha's name and hearing...

If even those who merely hear its name can be born there and achieve the path of Buddhahood, how much more so for those who, throughout their lives, wear it upon their heads and uphold it with all their might!
Indeed, the various sufferings of this world are truly beyond description, while the manifold joys of that land are a true bliss that cannot be fully exhausted.
The difference between heaven and earth is as vast as the distance between them; thus, superiority and inferiority are naturally revealed.

Therefore, one should know that among those within the three realms, there is no one who ought not to urgently exit the burning house and swiftly enter the lotus pond to leave birth and death behind, rather than waiting for the fruit of Buddhahood.

Whenever I contemplate the suffering of the five turbidities in this Sahā world, I rejoice in the Pure Land and loathe this realm of suffering, hurrying to return to the bliss of the nine grades of rebirth in An-yang, and abandoning [this world].

To leave the prison of the womb and enter the lotus pond, one must employ fierce right mindfulness to sweep away distracted thoughts, dilute the flavor of the world, and thicken the flavor of the Buddha.
This is done solely for the purpose of escaping this Saha world. To escape the Saha world, one must contemplate the Buddha with single-minded purity.

To contemplate the Buddha with single-minded purity, one must sever the turbid stream. When the turbid stream ceases, the sufferings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are instantly stilled. Contemplate!
The Buddha’s purity is such that he has abandoned retributive existence for wondrous bliss and tranquility; therefore, he does not sever his worldly ties.

If one cuts off the turbid flow [of worldly attachments], yet fails to make the mind purely clean and the thoughts purely unified, how could one possibly achieve resonance while contemplating Amitābha?
It is like a straight form producing a distorted shadow, or a turbid source resulting in murky currents. Viewed from this perspective, one cannot help but prune away its branches.

He severed [the ties of worldly life], removing its sprouts and shoots. He purified his six sense faculties and cleansed his three karmas. He constructed a thatched hut and secluded himself within a small room.
Restraining body and mind, he maintained this practice with diligence until the end of the year.

From dawn until dusk, throughout the six periods of day and night, he constantly contemplated returning to the Pure Land. Burning incense and offering his fingers, everything was done as a vow to seek [rebirth].

Having been born [in this world], I shall reveal my faults with diligence and earnestly strive to expiate all transgressions and evils. How could I fear exhaustion? May there be no interval between cold and warmth.

Even if the karma of the past and present is heavy, or the obstacles of many kalpas are deep, such that I cannot reach the goal within this very body, I vow to serve as a monk in every lifetime and to practice mindfulness of the Buddha without interruption, following the golden words of Kāśyapa and Amitābha.
This is my great vow. May all those born by virtue of the compassionate light enter everywhere into [the path], and through various skillful means, deliver sentient beings.
Even if empty space should come to an end, my vow shall be inexhaustible. With the utmost sincerity of my humble heart, I respectfully draft this brief preface.

My vulgar words are yet unrefined and these rough rhymes are hastily composed. My craftsmanship is clumsy and my learning is shallow; may those who read this kindly forgive me for not laughing at it. Still...
I hope for your compassionate instruction. I look up to you and beg for your pity;
please take me swiftly to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*), so that I may avoid being ground down by manifold sufferings.

I am ashamed that I am like a scorched sprout or a rotten seed—my afflictions are truly many. Fortunately, there is the Compassionate Vessel to rescue me; when I call upon its name, suffering immediately ceases.
I pray that Your Majesty will graciously take me in; Carrying my karma, I depart from this Sahā world.
Seeking to leave the path of Sahā, First I shall clear away the thorns and ailments. When the poisonous roots are all cut clean, The branches and leaves will naturally vanish.
With a single mind, never distracted, I shall hold fast to Amitābha.
Pure and free from even the slightest habituation, With retribution fulfilled, one hides within the lotus calyx.

Reflecting on the suffering of the three realms, One turns toward the Great Enlightened Immortal. Urgently seeking escape from the burning house, One must take the practice of Buddha-remembrance as primary.
If accomplishment is attained merely by hearing the name, How much more so for those who uphold the sixty thousand [verses]?
Following the sutras and relying on the Buddha’s words, one should make faith and aspiration firm and pure;
this is the true peace and bliss of the Pure Land, the most supreme condition for rebirth there.

It is vital to cultivate a profound sense of joy in the Pure Land and revulsion toward this world, while continuously reciting the six characters. With every thought, let the mind be single-minded; with every sound, the Buddha appears before you.
When mindfulness reaches the day of the Fragrant Melon, I vow to enter the lowest grade of lotus (as the sutra says: even birth in the lowest grade surpasses the rank of celestial officials;
how much more so the middle, upper, and highest grades!).
Furthermore, there are four stanzas in five lines of seven characters each:
The burning house of the three realms belongs to my own body; The three karmas, in their delusion, are created by myself (*Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"All is created only by the mind"). I have traversed boundless paths of evil.
From suffering to suffering until now, my compassionate father has guided me; only now do I realize my remorse.
My mind was poisoned by greed, hatred, and delusion, but through the Buddha’s nectar, my obscurations have been cleansed;
my chronic ailments have diminished, and I am gradually returning to health.
My illness should have brought death; how fortunate that I live! It relies entirely upon the Unsurpassed Honored One, the King of Physicians.
One must strive with urgency to hold his name; By practicing this oneself and encouraging others, one repays his compassionate grace.
The dangers and afflictions of this Sahā world are truly loathsome and terrifying; The peace and security of the Pure Land are truly enviable and joyful.
I vow that at the end of life, I shall sever all paths; With right mindfulness, I shall enter directly and ascend toward the West.
Having been born there, I shall return again to the Sahā world, Proclaiming the Dharma everywhere to repay the Buddha’s kindness.
With ten billion emanations, I shall widely exhort and guide, Using various skillful means to deliver sentient beings.
Responding spontaneously to transform beings without weariness, you manifest expedient supernatural powers to pull them from the fire.
I only pray that those of the four modes of birth may return to the pure realm; may the lotus roots fully develop according to the original aspiration.
The Buddha’s compassionate vows are wondrous and immeasurable; even if one were to exhaust all boundless gates of skillful means—
Only the Land of Bliss is called most supreme; Most supreme and extraordinary, it delivers people across the sea of suffering.
It brings the deluded children to enlightenment and joy at the Lotus Pond. To begrudge and defile this treasure is to cause oneself grievous pain.
Knowing that the other realm is so wondrous, Even celestial beings vow to fly there and be reborn.

If one asks, "What is it that the celestial deities desire to be born into? the answer is found in the sutras: "When the merits of heavenly bliss are exhausted, one still falls into the three miserable realms.

Therefore, it is better to renounce the celestial palaces and hasten to return to the Pure Land. This clearly demonstrates that while the joys of the celestial courts are superior, one’s rank there remains subject to non-retrogression;
yet even there, one may never fall. One must realize that this is the case for the celestial deities themselves—how much more so for the meager existence of human beings!
Is this not a form of sustenance? Yet, you, who are lost, do not perceive your own stinginess and attachment; you are like bees clinging to flowers or ants yearning for their nests.

You take pride in impurity and consider the meager to be sufficient. How is this any different [from the worldly]? It is truly lamentable that some are so foolish as to remain ignorant, while others, though possessing wisdom, fail to awaken;
and those who have awakened yet harbor no aspiration—these are deeply pitiable. This is the way of human beings.

If one does not penetrate through, what path can there be for escape? If one is content to wander back and forth in the sea of suffering, traversing perilous paths, and has no desire to return to the source or attain rebirth, I do not know where such a person will go.
In the western direction of this Sahā world, the two realms of suffering and pleasure are clearly distinguished as superior and inferior; each is described in ten chapters.
One should loathe and abandon the former, while delighting in and adopting the latter. Regarding the sentiments of suffering in the Sahā world, it says:
Abandon the five turbidities swiftly; do not be stingy or procrastinate. Various sufferings burn one simultaneously, joint by joint. The eight difficulties and three calamities constantly meet;
famine and pestilence increase day by day. (Unless one leaves the triple world, no person can avoid them.)
Time passes like an arrow and life is truly brief; change and impermanence occur in the space of a moment.

If you do not urgently seek the path to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang), there will be no end to suffering as you pass from birth here to death there—every transition is nothing but suffering.
We exchange pleasantries year after year; this feeling originally stems entirely from Heaven. When heat comes, how is it different from glowing coals?
When cold departs, even frost and ice are pitiable (if even cold and heat are so difficult to endure, how much more so the other sufferings?).
The world’s quest for food and clothing is a suffering difficult to describe; one rushes through waves of misery, braving rain and fierce winds.

If one can grow weary of this suffering and diligently recite the Buddha’s name, the precious treasures in the Land of Bliss are most abundant there (whereas in other realms, food and clothing arrive spontaneously without effort; would one not rather take the jewels than discard the pebbles?).
A single measure of grain is hard to find; beyond one's lot, there is bitter suffering. Morning comes without evening; truly, one is empty and famished.

This is because of extreme stinginess in past lives; thus, one encounters retribution in this life as deprivation and exhaustion (if there is no sowing in spring, how can there be harvesting in autumn?).
Lifting one's eyes, one frequently beholds the forms of evil people; their hundreds of wily stratagems are beyond hearing. Easy to create at the time [of action], but bitter when retribution falls.

When the King examines the case and the court reviews the dossier, how can there be room for sentiment? (Who among those who call themselves men of noble character knows what it is to be a prisoner? Yet in other realms there is not even the name of "evil," let alone the sight of its form.
Therefore, one should recollect the Buddha and hasten thither.)

The ferocity of jackals and wolves may still be avoided, but when the three poisons dwell within one’s heart, they are most difficult to guard against. The wise person devotes themselves exclusively to the practice of morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*);

thus the eight deviations and ten evils will vanish to other realms. (In every movement and stillness, one must be exceedingly attentive. Even if a tiger were to let loose, the harm it would inflict on people would not be slight. Be cautious; be observant!)
Boundless evil realms have already been traversed; having been pulled by the bone and stripped of the sinew, one has arrived at this human body, which is not easily attained.

For what reason do you still not urgently seek birth [in the Way]? (Transmigrating through the six paths, one does not escape the womb, egg, moisture, or transformation; thus one must inevitably pass through them all. Now that you have become human, you should swiftly pursue the root.)

Suffering in form, suffering in circumstance, and suffering in emotion abound; the suffering is beyond words, so what can be done? One can only harbor a heart of pain and diligently recite the Buddha’s name.
To transform suffering into joy is the mark of a hero (the two characters for "reciting the Buddha's name" [nien-fo] are not something that even great men cannot do; therefore, he is a hero.
He must certainly be able to harbor a heart of pain, for the suffering of this Sahā world can only be saved by the Buddha; thus, one should recite the Buddha’s name).
I sigh deeply over the suffering of the beings in this Sahā world; I urge you to quickly emerge and swiftly leave this pit.

It requires nothing more than a sincere and earnest faith in the Western Land; with ten recitations of Amitābha’s name, one shall attain rebirth there. (If you do not escape this pit, then regardless of whether you are a king above or an ant below, all are alike within it.
Whether enduring bitterness or seeking pleasure, spending your days thus—what joy is there in such a state?)
The scenery of the Western Land of Bliss is described as follows:
"One may freely choose among the nine lotus-pools to dwell in that Land of Happiness. Its bliss is ineffable and rare in this world. Clothing and food appear spontaneously without effort;

its precious jewels are beyond measure—truly marvelous! (When comparing this to other realms, the difference is as vast as heaven and earth. The joys within it could not be fully proclaimed even in a hundred kalpas. Do you know this?)"

The radiance and lifespan are both immeasurable; there is no distinction between long and short among those who have gone [there]. Those in their final birth before Buddhahood are all non-retrogressive;
the assembly of supreme virtues gathers together, each excelling in strength. (The people of that land are equal in their lifespans and dispositions, all of which are difficult to measure.)
The ground is of pure gold, exceedingly majestic and beautiful. Celestial music welcomes him from the void as he honors Amitābha; each brings exquisite flowers to present as offerings.
The billions of Buddhas of other lands all look toward him with reliance (flowing unceasingly throughout the six periods of day and night).
Beside the ponds of the seven treasures stand many exquisite terraces; the tiered pavilions are truly magnificent and grand.
A gentle breeze stirs the rows of trees, and the Arhats enjoying their merit smile broadly upon their faces. (As for this merit and worldly merit, how do they compare in quality?)
Exquisite and variegated multitudes of spiritual birds emit harmonious and elegant sounds that delight the hearts of all beings; naturally, they all conceive the thought of the Buddha-Dharma.
These manifested transformations—how could they be among the animals? (Since these are not born of karmic retribution for sin, they are created by Amitābha.)
The immeasurable and boundless assembly of śrāvakas were all utterly sincere in their mindfulness of the Buddha.

How could one know that among the men and women of this turbid age, there might not be those who cannot achieve birth [in the Pure Land]? (Since he was a great man, so am I; as long as the heart is earnest, everything can be accomplished.)

Utterly free from even the slightest suffering and consisting purely of all joys, it is easy to reach yet no one goes there—how truly pitiable! It pains me to the core that the King of Vows must gaze upon this with eyes broken by sorrow;
the deluded child sleeps soundly amidst the bitterness of yellow myrobalan (clinging to suffering while abandoning joy—their delusion is profound indeed).
How could the wondrous realm of the Land of Bliss ever be exhausted? Infinite and boundless, it is penetrated by a single contemplation.

Pure, partless, and luminous, the entire reality is fully manifested; this very mind is Buddha, dwelling within it (regarding the four characters "this mind is Buddha," do not regard them with a casual attitude).
By recollecting the Buddha at the moment of death, one attains a wondrous cause; the Great Being Amitābha will personally come to welcome them.

In the space of a single thought, they enter the lotus womb; as soon as dawn breaks, joy fills my heart this morning. (Had I known it would be thus, I would have practiced from birth; now I regret it is too late. May all you virtuous ones believe this with gladness!)

Briefly praising the sentiment of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss: Quickly and diligently apply yourself to the mindfulness of the Buddha like a spark of fire. Cease clinging to the filthy food within the ant-hill;

Speedily proceed to the lotus pedestal to enjoy the supreme delicacies. (Since there are such wondrous places as these, if you again willingly cling to that burning house, begrudge its rubble, and do not aspire for rebirth there, I say that you will certainly have no time of escape.)
Indeed, the suffering of this Sahā world and the joy of the Western Land are truly and undeniably so;
even if one were to use the mouths of those throughout the ten directions, they could not fully express them. Since there is such a distinction between suffering and joy, I ask you:
would you rather willingly remain attached to a realm of suffering, or would you urgently seek to realize the causes of joy? Between these two, there is only...

Let this be known by the wise; do not follow the path of the foolish. Some may say that this is a fabrication of Padma (Lotus) and thus should not be trusted because of its association with wicked people.
I answer: Although it is called a fabrication, it has been examined throughout history;

it is pointed out by a thousand scriptures and proclaimed by ten thousand Buddhas. Since this is not the fault of the narrator, could it possibly be contrary to the scriptures or the Buddhas? Alas! O Buddha...

If one’s words are not believed, what words can be trusted? If the Way of humanity is not cultivated, what Way can be cultivated? (I) shall once more rend my heart and dig out my lungs with these words: If my wisdom is good yet my heart harbors even a trace of deceit, may I immediately fall into the plow-drawn hells. If I offer this sincere heart to you, sirs, I pray that you will quickly leave the Sahā world and vow to enter the Western Paradise. To those who say they do not believe, I address them from the ten directions: [The following is the verse: If you do not believe, I shall cut open my chest and pull out my heart; If you do not believe, I shall gouge out my liver and lungs. If you do not believe, I shall burn my body as an offering; If you do not believe, I shall cast myself into the fire. If you do not believe, I shall cut off my head and offer it as a gift; If you do not believe, I shall sever my limbs and present them as tribute. If you do not believe, I shall grind my bones to powder; If you do not believe, I shall crush my flesh into paste. If you do not believe, I shall offer my eyes and ears; If you do not believe, I shall give my nose and tongue. If you do not believe, I shall offer my hands and feet; If you do not believe, I shall surrender my brain and marrow. If you do not believe, I shall offer my blood and tears; If you do not believe, I shall give my skin and flesh. If you do not believe, I shall offer my breath and voice; If you do not believe, I shall surrender my spirit and soul. Even all the Buddhas have nothing they can do about it; how much less so a solitary mountain-dwelling śrāmaṇera who has broken the precepts?

Regarding the character for "mind" (*citta*), it is said: "How great is this mind! How wondrous is this mind! "Great" takes its meaning from its essential nature; "wondrous" takes its meaning from its spontaneous functioning.
Taking destiny as its essence, it can encompass the Great Void and its measure extends throughout the realms of sand;

truly, this is not a mind of fleshly aggregates or deluded thought, but rather the mind of the radiance of wisdom—this is what is called "the mind. This mind transcends emptiness and existence while embodying all principles;
it surpasses sound and form while responding to myriad affairs. Even were there as many brilliant talents as the sands of the Ganges, they could not fathom it.

How wise! Indeed, there is no phenomenon, whether mundane or supramundane, that does not arise from this mind. Whether one becomes a sage or a worthy person, none do so without being accomplished through this mind.
As the *Zhongyong* says, "That which must not be left for even a moment" is precisely this mind.

It is like a minister serving his sovereign or a son serving his father; it should not be departed from for even a foot or an inch. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "One should contemplate the Dharma-realm..."

Nature: All is created solely by the mind. One must know that what is created solely by the mind includes the attainment of sagehood and worthiness, as well as all causes and conditions of good and evil;
none of these arise apart from this mental consciousness, which produces the various karmic retributions of ascent and descent, suffering and joy.
Therefore, a single thought that arises within our present minds—if it does not fall into the Buddha-realm (buddha-dhātu), it falls into the nine realms.
As for these nine realms: the Buddha-realm, the Bodhisattva-realm, the Perfect Enlightenment-realm (pariniṣpanna-bodhi-dhātu), and the Śrāvaka-realm constitute the four noble realms.
Next, the celestial realm, the human realm, and the asura realm, along with the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals, constitute the six [worldly] realms.
Generally, all who possess a mind have thoughts. However, those who have thoughts never transcend these ten dharma-realms within the mind.
Therefore, if the mind recollects the Buddha, it will certainly fall into the Buddha-realm; if the mind recollects anything else...
That one does not transcend the nine realms is because each and every one of them is produced by a single thought within this mind; thus, one falls into those nine realms.
It is like a shadow that must follow a form, or a current that must follow its source: if the form is upright, the shadow is straight;
if the source is turbid, the current is murky. What the sutras mean by "all things are created solely by the mind" is that there is no phenomenon outside of the mind.
"Outside the Dharma there is no mind. This means that apart from the present single thought of ours, there is not even a hair’s breadth of a dharma upon which one can stand.

Alas! Regarding this single word "mind," there is such a vast difference between heaven and abyss, such a disparity between superior and inferior, and such variations between rising and sinking, suffering and joy.
Truly, it is not that the person does not treasure it; it is not that they do not treasure it, for it is the person who is not [truly] human. Therefore, wisdom—
This refers to being cautious when alone. One must maintain awareness in every thought-moment, borrowing this provisional body before it perishes to cultivate the Real.

Cease all evils to honor manifold virtues; practice skillful means to deliver all living beings. Furthermore, one should realize that time and light are easily lost, and awaken to the fact that life is as difficult to retain as a spark struck from stone.
The body is like drifting clouds, and life is like a candle in the wind. Since even a single breath is difficult to preserve, how [can one afford to be negligent]?
If you have committed various unwholesome deeds, you must urgently cultivate faith and recite the Buddha’s name.

Even if you cannot yet leave the household life, you should find moments of leisure amidst your busyness and recite a few phrases of Amitābha Buddha’s name. Gradually, plant even a small amount of this most supreme wholesome cause.
If you can sever worldly attachments and suspend all affairs, believe deeply that this very mind is originally the Buddha.
This beginningless delusion and obscurity has led us to suffering until this very day. Now that you have attained a slight awakening, you should establish a firm vow:

from this moment forth, sweep away all remaining worldly studies and apply yourself with single-minded urgency to the study of the Buddha. Even unto the point where your breath ceases and your legs go straight, do not allow yourself the slightest alteration or slackening.
If you can maintain such deep faith, it will not be difficult to face the Buddha before long. Nevertheless, the two characters for "cultivation" (xiūxíng) truly possess no other meaning.

In the Dharma, what is valued is the upholding of the precepts and the recitation of the Buddha’s name. Furthermore, these two words, "reciting the Buddha's name," possess nothing particularly extraordinary;
what is valued is sincerity and single-mindedness. What is meant by sincerity and single-mindedness? It refers to the simultaneous establishment of faith, aspiration, and practice as a triad.

If one’s faith is sincere, one will certainly sever all doubts. If one’s aspiration is sincere, one will certainly escape the Saha world. If one’s practice is sincere, one will certainly reach the Western Land and draw near to the Buddha.

This is certainly so. As for the statement in the *Amitābha Sūtra* that "this mind is Buddha," it was the Great Compassionate Original Teacher Śākyamuni who clearly revealed that every person can become a Buddha through this very mind.
Since he has already granted that every person can become a Buddha, how could one discard this further and fall into delusion once more?
Therefore, one should rely upon this illusory physical form and apply oneself with earnest resolve and diligence.
Truly, if one reads the Buddha’s teachings and pays homage to the Buddha, at the time of one’s future death, one will certainly behold the Buddha.
If the mind is thus, and one gives rise to this thought, then the nine realms will be completely severed and one will surely descend into the Buddha-realm. Therefore it is said:
"How wondrous is this single thought of the mind! Those who understand this principle, even if they dwell in a royal palace or a celestial palace, [are not bound by them].

They take this as a cause for joy. Why? Because their heavenly blessings are finite. As the sutra says: "When the enjoyment of heavenly blessings is exhausted, one falls back into the midst of insects on the hump of an ox.
How much more so regarding the meager fortunes and rewards of the human realm! Furthermore, it is said that in the West, there is the lowest-of-the-low grade.

It is already superior to the celestial palaces; how much more so for those of the highest grade! Therefore, you should quickly give rise to faith and single-mindedly and earnestly practice these essential points.
If I were not to follow the Buddha’s words and instead spoke from my own whims to deceive you, gentlemen, may my fragrance of precepts immediately fall into the plow-field of hell.
Since this is truly so, I exhort you all: believe deeply, for this mind can indeed be realized.

If you, virtuous ones, desire that we all together descend into the Buddha-realm, then I pray that once this present retribution-body is exhausted, I may swiftly be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss, so that I may soon behold Amitābha, soon dwell in the Pure Land, soon return to the Sahā world, and soon come to transform and deliver others.
I earnestly hope that you sages will not reject these words because of the person who speaks them, lest you辜负 (gu fu) your own hearts; I entreat you to taste these words with quiet reflection.
All may, by means of this mind, cross the ocean of suffering; by means of this mind, ascend to the Land of Bliss;
