by means of this mind, give rise to inexhaustible merit and wisdom; and by means of this mind, dwell upon the lotus seats of the highest grade. Alas!
If this is so, what could be more supreme and joyful than this throughout the great earth? Who indeed could surpass it?
In my leisure from meditation, I ask myself: what is meant by "shining-skull"?
Originally, one who shaves their head and dyes their robes, with a radiant scalp and bare feet, is called a *arhat* free from desire, a superior gentleman who has transcended the mundane world.

Transcending all sensory dusts, one cuts off the various realms of existence; awakening to the three voids, one surmounts the triple world. Fame and profit are utterly severed; honor and disgrace are non-existent.
Beholding the crimson of peach blossoms and the green of willows, one perceives them as lasting but a single decade;

hearing the sounds of the ocean assembly and the lotus pond, one knows them all to be superior friends—far more so than any kin. What concern have they for the passage of spring and autumn? By nature, one is like a leisurely person beyond the mundane world.
How can one compare this to a mere worldly guest? Alas, how can one overcome such deep-seated and thick habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) that they do not fade away without effort?
It is like the black feathers of a crow or the webbed entanglements of a spider; it is certainly not something produced by artificial means, nor does it depend on human labor.

Because their ignorance fills their bellies and their habitual tendencies fill their chests, they are habituated solely to rushing outward in pursuit; how could there be any internal practice of right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*)?

Using offerings as a pretext for socializing, they inquire after one’s health at inappropriate times; they gather in groups by feigning mountain retreats and form crowds under the guise of Dharma assemblies.

Monastics and laypeople jostle together, men and women mingle in confusion. How can such outward appearances be considered elegant? They fail to establish the regulations of the Śākya clan and cannot avoid public censure.
How could this possibly uphold the standards of the Sangha? Viewed in this light, it flagrantly violates the Buddha’s precepts; yet it is not a transgression of the Vinaya.
[The conduct of] ritual observances is fixed in violation of the *śīla*. How can the people of the world believe it? How can they digest even a grain of rice [offered by them]?
Alas! Such is the state of the Dharma-ending age (*mappō*). Would not all the Buddhas not feel sorrow for this? We, too, suffer and are caught up within its midst.

Deeply ashamed of our own ignorance and folly, we hide our heads and shrink our necks; thus, fearing the countenances of others, we seek refuge in mountain forests. Truly, there is nothing that can be done.
I am capable [of this]. I am merely a beginner who reads the Buddha’s teachings; yet I alone have two habits that differ slightly from those of others:
namely, my fear of clamor and confusion, which harm the wholesome Dharma and injure ethical discipline (*śīla*);

and my fear of slighting virtuous friends, which causes moral integrity to decline, as well as momentary laziness and the sudden ceasing of the Buddha’s voice, for time passes with the speed of lightning.
Furthermore, one's life depends on the breath. When the time of death approaches, one is overwhelmed by the groans of suffering and pain.

Yet, those who follow next [in the hierarchy of practice] are joyful because they are free from worldly attachments, are pure and tranquil, diminish the evil realms, and strictly observe the rules of discipline.
I revere the wearing of coarse garments and cherish the merit of even a single needle; I dare not allow the slightest negligence.

I maintain the recitation of the Buddha’s name with focused diligence so that I may swiftly leave the ocean of suffering and quickly ascend to the other shore. At the time of casting off this physical existence, my demeanor was serene as I passed away.
To abandon these base habits of joy and fear is not something my studies would permit, nor is it something I can reconcile with.

This is my aspiration. Yet, should one wish to repay the Buddha’s original intent and move Maitreya to welcome them, nothing is more sublime than cultivating the pure practice of the Uninterrupted Path (*anantara-karma*).
Those who cultivate the pure practice of the Uninterrupted Path must follow the instructions of the Great Master Shandao:
"With the body, single-mindedly prostrate to Amitābha Buddha; with the mouth, single-mindedly recite the name of Amitābha Buddha; and with the mind, single-mindedly contemplate Amitābha Buddha."
This is so. It means that one’s body, speech, and mind shall never at any time fail to be in the Pure Land, and never for a single moment fail to be in the presence of the Buddha.

Furthermore, if one maintains the practice of both joy and fear throughout one’s entire life without ceasing—essentially encompassing the Buddha’s compassionate embrace—one will certainly be moved by Amida.
If one were to abandon this and instead devise some other extraordinary practice, I truly do not know what it might be like.
Therefore, when it comes to "shining on the bald head," one must first recognize the [head] itself. If you ultimately do not know it, what does it mean to say "shining on the bald head"?

This is truly a matter of the utmost pity. It is like a scholar entering the examination hall who, having no knowledge of the head [of the paper], how could he possibly compose an essay, let alone hope to ascend the honor roll?
The same applies to the bald head: from the moment of tonsure, one is like a blind person.

I have wandered aimlessly, bumping into things at random from east to west, until today I still do not know what I have been doing. My speech lacks any sense of principle, and my discourse is devoid of historical precedent.
As the Master Zheng Xingong says in his *Pure Land Poems*: "When one is deluded at the first step, one is deluded at every step. This is precisely it.
Had I encountered a worthy person who guided me toward the recitation of the Buddha's name, I would have said that the Western Path is far away, and I—
How could they possibly reach it? Some may acquire slight skills and claim that they have already mastered the Buddha-dharma;

others, receiving the protection and assistance of faithful donors, boastfully say, "I possess the merit of cultivation. Thus, their vision is like that of a goose, giving rise to great arrogance (*māna*).

Even if they see those of integrity and noble yielding, such people do not fall within the range of their gaze, because they focus exclusively on power and influence and are habituated to craving fame and profit. This is so.
Because they are utterly devoid of shame and utterly lacking in a sense of remorse, alas! Amidst such suffering and affliction, how could they know they are ill?
Once the light of their eyes falls, they will undergo torment for hundreds of kalpas; it requires nothing more than to ask oneself—why trouble the Lord Yama with judgment?

At that time, if one wishes again to become a monk, it will be as difficult to fulfill this wish as it is to prevent a calamity. Therefore, the wise hear this and weep in pain, while the foolish merely hear it.
This leads to resentment because our choices differ; it is merely a matter of private versus public interests.
Alas! If this is the case, I shall question you: since you have left your parents and kin, severed your ties with your six relations, and shaved your head, what exactly is the purpose of all this?
When questioned thus repeatedly, why do you remain speechless with a fixed gaze? It is utterly [absurd].

He did not allow for any retort. Again, with a stern voice, he struck the table once and asked a single question, as if five thunderbolts were shaking his crown and a hundred arrows were piercing his heart.
Suddenly, his heart trembled and his hair stood on end; sweat and tears flowed together. It was as if he had taken several doses of *chái-hú* medicine or several courses of decoctions;
the long-standing stupor finally awakened, and the various chronic ailments were somewhat relieved. Thus, he was interrogated with relentless prodding for the rest of his life, even though...
When the grasses and trees grieve at the moat, one who is cautious in solitude feels such piercing sorrow that even a stubborn rock is moved to anguish.

One must know that if this is so for insentient things, how much more so for those endowed with empty spirit and unclouded awareness? Therefore, one gives rise to great terror and profound shame. As the Sūtra says:
"A human body is difficult to obtain, like casting a mustard seed onto the point of a needle; the Buddha-dharma is difficult to encounter, like a blind turtle [seeking a hole in a floating log]."
To encounter a floating log is rare; it is difficult even to obtain a human body, let alone the Buddha-dharma.
Now that I have obtained this human body and am further favored by the ranks of the Sangha, having received the full precepts, I am truly fortunate throughout a thousand lifetimes.

If I do not take advantage of this retributive body to leave the sea of suffering early and seek birth in a Land of Bliss, what other body shall I wait for to be born again? What life will I have to live again?
Yet, once the *kāṣāya* is lost, it will be difficult to encounter again for ten thousand kalpas. Moreover, human life is impermanent; it cannot be guaranteed for even a single breath.
One dwells but briefly in the human realm, while the underworld is one's eternal abode. I shall provide another analogy and ask you this:

suppose there were two people in the world, both of whom find it difficult to remain alive. One has violated the laws of the state and is led to the marketplace to await execution; the other suffers from a terminal illness.

"Suppose there are two people suffering from severe illness, about to be cast into blazing flames and hot embers. Since their hearts have not yet ceased, they will surely think of rescue and pardon, and they will certainly desire to escape with their lives.

Even if one were to offer them a beautiful wife and lovely concubines, children and precious treasures, as well as hundreds of varieties of delicacies for their enjoyment—allowing those two to take whatever they desired according to their own wishes—would they still be able to turn their consciousness toward such things with longing? He replied, "Because of that..."
Life lasts but a moment; with the sole thought of escaping death, how could one dare give rise to a heart that looks back with desire?
There has never been such a person in all the world who disregards their own life while remaining foolishly attached to it.

Should such a person exist, they would be a candidate for death in the truest sense, whom even the thousand Buddhas could hardly save—how much less so you and I! Alas! How exquisite this analogy is! This is the question.
I answer: You must know that even one's own life is difficult to preserve; how much more so, then, can one covet illusory things? It is the same for those who merely shave their heads:
as long as they have not clarified the Great Matter, they cannot escape birth and death; they have not yet left the sea of suffering, nor have they reached the other shore.
To fail to earnestly practice the mindfulness of the Buddha, while instead neglecting one’s own spiritual life to crave all manner of worldly affairs and sensual pleasures—this is truly folly.

How utterly foolish! It is the height of folly. Therefore, the wise are not like this; they should emulate those two [the Buddha and his disciples] in their resolve, diligently practice pure deeds, and seek liberation at the moment of death as if fearing execution or being beset by water and fire, calling the Buddha's name with all their might.

Devoting oneself solely to escaping the cycle of birth and death, how could one dare to allow even a hair’s breadth of negligence, let alone cling to worldly ties, engage in miscellaneous affairs, or seek outward respectability?

How could such a person be called capable or wise? If, upon realizing this is truly so, one awakens and earnestly practices the recitation of the Buddha’s name, I grant that such a person shall point to the day of their birth as the day they will be born in the Western Pure Land;
it may be said that they stand face-to-face with the Buddha in this very life. Therefore, once you have become a shaven-headed monk, you must resolutely sever [worldly attachments].

Regarding worldly conditions: having severed the ties to wealth and beauty, I am indifferent to celestial maidens or the moon’s hare-mark; even all the world’s treasures, up to and including the throne of a king, I do not consider extraordinary.
Should I encounter those who come specifically to test me or seduce me, my heart shall remain as firm as iron and stone.
I regard evil wealth as pebbles and evil beauty as maggots—things unsuitable for a śramaṇa like myself. I would rather die than concern myself with them.
This is for one’s own spiritual life. These words constitute the primary gateway for those with shaven heads; they are a vital certificate.

Whether one’s fate lies in life or death, in black or white, truly rests upon this. This applies not only to followers of the Śākya clan, but even Confucians ought to maintain what falls within their own domain.

Why should they covet that which lies outside it? Thus, we know that there are none who, having lost their integrity and violated their principles, do not treat their bodies lightly and subject themselves to such trials.
Because of these two characters, "wealth" and "beauty," one’s lifelong reputation and integrity are cast into a pit or a latrine.

How much more so for one with the dignified appearance of a monk, who has fully received the Buddha’s precepts, ought to listen to the Buddha’s words, and must abide by the Buddha’s regulations; even grinding teeth in determination, one would rather die than violate them.
Someone might say: "Your 'fragrance of the precepts' is but the narrow vision of a *śrāmaṇera*. One who practices the Bodhisattva path possesses wisdom that fills [their being] and power..."
Zu said, "The Dharma is indeed without obstruction. Let me ask you this: Are you a bodhisattva?

If you enter and exit hell, amidst spears, halberds, and swords, or within filth and excrement, and even if you take fire and water as your home, can you do so without obstruction, without constraint, and without fear?
If it is so, then it is truly as you say. However, if there is even the slightest obstruction, I hope you will not trouble yourself to speak such pleasing words."
Yet we willingly fall into the deep abyss. One must realize that you and I are ordinary beings bound by all fetters;

if even a slight fragment of illness makes it difficult for us to maintain mastery over ourselves, how much more so when faced with the thousandfold entanglements of extreme suffering that are difficult to endure?

This is truly because, from the time one enters the path of study until reaching the position of a ruler, and from the stage of a *śrāmaṇera* until attaining Buddhahood, there is nothing that does not begin with the first step. It is like a journey of a thousand li; [it begins] at the opening...
To walk astray is to lose one's way; how then can one reach the path ahead?

Since my fragrant precepts have already failed in filial piety, those who act as śramaṇas ought to obey the Buddha’s commands, ought to observe the Buddha’s precepts, and ought to follow the Buddha’s conduct—these three points alone constitute the very title of being a "shaven-headed" one.
One must recognize things clearly, guard against them with firm resolve, read until mastery is achieved, and memorize with steadfastness;

only then, when composing essays, poems, or rhapsodies, will one invariably succeed in passing the examinations. Otherwise, there will be no grounds for renown. Therefore, one must urgently establish one's own vows and aspirations:

to follow along with the favorable and harmonious while using the adverse to turn them into the favorable; to make the unfamiliar familiar and to transform the familiar into the unfamiliar. This is how it should be.
Although my humble view is not particularly extraordinary, I ask that you savor it in stillness and examine it thoroughly;

if it corresponds with reality, then, as for the question, "Since you are devoted exclusively to the Pure Land, why do you engage in such elaborate proliferation?"—you should simply cut through all such entanglements and be old-fashioned and straightforward.
It is sufficient to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha until the end. It is fitting that you exhaust this present life with a single moment of uninterrupted focus;

one must strictly avoid mixed practice or miscellaneous deeds. Beginning from this very day, practice with earnest resolve until the breath ceases, never altering your approach by even a hair’s breadth.
If you can exert yourself in this way with such fervent aspiration, on the day the fragrance of the melon ripens, you will surely behold Amitābha face-to-face.
At the moment the lotus bud falls, they are reborn in the Pure Land.

Furthermore, for the sake of their parents, teachers, and elders from beginningless time, as well as their karmic creditors—whether enemies or kin—one performs great Buddhist rites and cultivates all manner of merit on their behalf.
This is because it causes one to transcend and enter the Pure Land. Thus, we know that the merit of mindfulness of the Buddha is inconceivable.
As for the discourse on self-benefit and the benefit of others, even all the Buddhas of the ten directions could not exhaustively describe it with their voices combined;
this is due to the power of the sixty-eight great vows that Amitābha Buddha made during his stage as a Bodhisattva. Consequently, there is no sentient being who is not encompassed by them.

There is nothing that does not benefit those who practice according to this. Those who attain faith with such intensity and achieve its practice with such singleness of purpose—those who sincerely and earnestly recite the name of the Buddha—should know that they have, from the beginning, possessed great roots of goodness, great merit, and great karmic conditions; only then can they possess such ultimate faith and profound practice.
Yet one must not be indolent or deluded; otherwise, delusion and indolence are unavoidable.

Therefore, having encountered such a benefit—like an infant biting its mother’s breast or a child climbing a vine—one must never let go even unto death. Whether one takes or abandons in the cycle of birth and death depends upon oneself;
how could it be obtained through the efforts of another? If one’s resolve is thus earnest and remains consistent from beginning to end, I dare say that one may truly be called [a practitioner].
The Way-man is acceptable; the Master is acceptable. Only then can one avoid bringing shame upon this bald head—these are the three characters [of my name].
Since I first took up the rank of monk by default, I have been ashamed of my ignorance, yet I have mistakenly continued in this path until now without any realization.
Even when beginners read the Buddha’s words, it is entirely like a mute man shouting at a woman; it is difficult to achieve resonance in ten thousand ways. Truly, this is shameful and painful.
How lamentable! How shameful! Because the days are long during the summer, I have composed these inquiries as a means of diversion during my studies.
My sole purpose is to prepare myself for lifelong investigation, so that I may further spur myself on until the end of my life. For this reason, I do not avoid coarse diction or vulgar phrasing;
I focus exclusively on self-interrogation and self-reproach. Alas! How I reproach myself!
My scalp is already bald; I shall renounce wealth and sever desire. Moderating my food and measuring my clothing, I shall live in simplicity and know contentment.
My pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) must be strictly purified; my discipline (*vinaya*) must not be deficient.
Time passes like a horse in a crevice; one must hasten to recollect the Buddha. This illusory body is not firm or enduring.
The difficulty of sustaining life through breath is certain; in an instant, impermanence arrives. Death is like a turtle shedding its shell—contemplate this carefully.
One will weep with terror and grief, for when one is alone and reflects on what must come, the heart and liver tear apart and hot blood flows.
This body is truly a source of suffering and affliction; how can one find joy in such a pit of deep attachment?
Within the five turbidities of this Sahā world, The three evil realms abound; Amidst a great accumulation of unwholesome deeds, I vow never again to be reborn here.
With resolute intent, I seek rebirth in that land, Determined to enter that realm, desiring the Buddha to extend his light to welcome me.
With sincerity, I revere the Buddha and recite his teachings, Placing deep faith in the words of all Buddhas.
The West is truly peaceful and blissful; this land is indeed perilous. At every moment one must guard against execution;
in this life there is no escape. By what body could one be released from prison? Better to die and enter the Land of Peaceful Nurturing than to lodge elsewhere.
With single-mindedness, contemplate Amitābha; Hold fast to his name without indolence or delusion.

Shedding tears, I recount these questions; throughout my life, I shall scourge my own bones. If I see or hear others rejoice in the Dharma, I shall further exhort them to do so, for this brings even greater merit.
For the third time, I shall close myself within retreat and read the verses on the Buddha’s rebirth in the Pure Land.
A single thatched cottage with six feet of cleared ground—unadorned, yet pure and refined. A hanging scroll of a Buddha image honors the Venerable Amitābha;
there is a single flower, a single lamp, and a single stick of incense. No stone chime is struck, no wooden fish is tapped.
With a single-minded focus, one sits or leans upon a rush mat, baring one's scalp and barefoot, wearing only a tattered robe.
I make my robes by day; at night, I shall wear but a single pair of trousers. Pickled vegetables and two bowls of thin congee—having ceased all greedy seeking, I am content and free from anxiety.
The door of my hermitage is always shut, and its panels are always barred. When meeting fellow practitioners, we converse; when gathering with pure friends, worldly guests are avoided.

I do not read the scholastic treatises nor peruse the sutras and verses, thereby conserving my eyesight and as it were avoiding idle distractions. Having cast away all dregs, there is nothing that is not right.

Regarding the flavor of dhyāna: simply discard speculative reasoning, discard delusive thoughts, and discard a distracted mind. Since there is neither honor nor disgrace, and one has severed fame and profit, having cast aside appearances, what constraints remain?

Feeling ashamed of my own incapacity, I study and recite the name of Amitābha. I vow to remain tranquil without ceasing; even when restless, I shall not abandon it; at death, I shall not depart from it.

May there be no interval between cold and warmth, and may I not avoid it even in sickness. For the rest of my life, I shall maintain this practice with all my strength, honoring the sixty thousand Buddhas.
Sorrow and delusion have come; I guard against the coming of the dim and obscure. My suffering is such that there is no one to study with and no meritorious practice.
I lack any foundation; it is pitiable and painful, shameful and disgraceful. It is not that Amitābha’s Original Vow is difficult to attain, yet I have failed to enter the pass once more.

I shall practice with earnestness without ceasing, resolutely seeking his radiance, seeking his compassion, and seeking deliverance. Until I ascend to the Land of Bliss and leave the sea of suffering behind, I shall sweep [away my defilements].

Other practitioners focus exclusively on worldly livelihoods rather than purely reciting the Buddha’s name; what is there to marvel at in that? You should instead read with sincerity, practice with sincerity, and uphold [the teachings] with sincerity.

This itself is the Supreme Vehicle. It is also called the "traveling expenses" for exhausting this present life to enter the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*), where you shall face Amitābha in person, pay homage directly to the Great Being (Avalokiteśvara), and—out of compassion for my fragrance of precepts—be granted a stroke upon the crown of your head and receive a prophecy of enlightenment. There, you shall assemble with all those of the highest rank.
"Excellent! Play with me until you have attained the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*). Do not abandon this; do not wish for another place, nor rely upon it.
This is my humble aspiration, my worthy wish, and what I have always delighted in."
A Song of Exhortation to Practice Single-mindedly with Diligence:

I urge you with bitter words—how excellent is the practice of nianfo! Abandon all other studies and miscellaneous practices entirely; focus exclusively on Amitābha. Seize this opportunity now while there is still time;
do not wait until the final moment when your feet are already stamping in haste. Do not engage in Zen meditation nor study the scriptures; the six characters are clearly the unsurpassed path.

The Way: Having encountered the King of Physicians, the sick child is fully cared for. Though one may grieve greatly over not yet having purchased the various medicinal herbs, there is no distinction between monastics and laity, old and young;
as long as one is willing to hold fast to the Name, one will ultimately be protected. If one can truly believe and practice with earnest aspiration, one will surely reach the goal.

What difference does it make whether one is noble or base, poor or wealthy? The body is like a bubble, life like a foam; arising and ceasing in an instant, it is not solid or firm. Behold the rising sun...
The sun rises in the east; before one realizes it, it has already set behind the western mountains. Be quick to reflect! You must hasten while you may.
A child in an instant becomes an old man. Coming empty-handed and kneeling barefoot, how shall you discharge the burden of karma upon your shoulders?
Were it not for the Buddha, who could provide protection? Recalling the Buddha is like pouring hot water upon snow. All conditioned phenomena are impermanent, like shadows flickering in the light.
Birth and death are as unpredictable as a single breath; one must truly regard them as such. Honor all that is good and sweep away all that is evil.

A drop of water can fill a great vessel; do not say it is too small. Good brings forth fortune, while evil invites calamity. Even the finest hair is clearly one’s own burden. Turn back quickly—do not delay!

The Way is early. Do not wait until you are thirsty before digging a well, lest you regret it later. While this physical strength and vitality remain, raise your eyebrows and quickly prepare thirty nights' worth of provisions.

Exhort both monastics and laypeople; when the sound of reciting the Buddha’s name does not cease, merit will soon be high. To do good is most joyful, but to recite the Buddha’s name is even more wondrous.
If one can recite a single phrase, that phrase is a treasure. The three karmas become pure and the six sense faculties become radiant, planting seeds for a vast harvest.

The sprouts of the immeasurable field of merit appear to be cultivated in a mixed manner, resulting in much suffering and little joy. Ultimately, it is better to uphold the precepts and recite the Buddha’s name.
Regarding the secret instructions for attending to those with chronic illnesses and assisting them toward a favorable rebirth at the end of life:
I have heard that birth and death are as ordinary for monastics and laypeople alike; they are inevitable aspects of living in this world. How can one allow... [the passage ends here].

Concerning Cold and Fever: These generally afflict ordinary beings bound by all fetters. Illnesses may be either provisional or ultimate. As for the provisional, these refer to ailments such as contracting wind-cold or having undigested food accumulation;
or cold-fever, heat-fever, pestilence, headaches, abdominal pains, and even extreme exhaustion, physical injury, sores, warts, dysentery, and the like.

Regarding these conditions, one should indeed seek prompt medical treatment and urgent care to preserve the vigor of the body, so that one may then apply oneself to spiritual practice. If, however, it is said to be ultimate...
Such a person has no medicine that can treat them; they will by no means be able to rise again. For the cultivation of one's lifespan is fixed, and life cannot be pulled back.
One must understand that medicine and physicians can only treat illness; they cannot treat life itself.
If medicine and physicians could treat life, it would be evident that those with wealth would never die. Thus, what is said regarding medicine and physicians is that they do not bring death.
Sickness. The Buddha saves those with whom he has a karmic connection. This clearly shows that when faced with the terminal illness of death, it is difficult to cure;

thus, it is further made evident that those who lack faith are difficult to save. Once one knows that one's life cannot be turned back, one should practice preliminary awakening and illumination, setting aside all the good and evil deeds performed throughout one’s life, both mentally and physically.
One need not expend mental effort trying to ensure a favorable outcome, nor should one harbor [fear].
With brows knit in sorrow and a heart chilled with apprehension, I leave it to him to ascend to heaven or fall to earth;

I simply maintain my hold upon one phrase: "Amitābha Buddha. As for everything else—be it the opening of heaven or the collapsing of the earth—it is none of my concern. I shall wait quietly for his departure.
Why? Because death is precisely birth. It is also called a "fortunate event," just as one discards tattered rags to exchange them for precious garments.
To don this [attire], to cast off the turbid waters of defilement and hasten toward the lotus pond, and to leave suffering behind to enter bliss—what cause for sorrow could there be?

If a sick person can thus suddenly become empty, thus let go, and thus contemplate the Dharma, never relaxing even for a moment upon the single phrase "Namu Amida Butsu" at the time of death, then even if there be karmic obstacles from past lives, they will not hinder them. Why is this? Because of that *amida*...

Amida Buddha made vows while on the path of practice; these will certainly not deceive anyone. His compassionate light will surely extend to draw you in and gather you into his embrace, so that you may be reborn according to your karma.
Therefore, there is no need for hesitation; simply maintain this resolve by firmly holding the Buddha’s name.
Nevertheless, although the patient may be able to remain steadfast in this way, at such a time they rely entirely upon those who assist in caring for them.
The Way is such that the sick person can only attend to their own pain and itching, and can only attend to reciting the Buddha’s name; they have no leisure to attend to other matters.
Therefore, those who provide care and assistance should show various forms of compassion and understanding. One must ensure that this effort does not begin but fail at the end.

According to the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, among the eight fields of merit, the field of merit of nursing the sick is the foremost field of merit. One must understand the significance of these two characters: "nursing the sick."
There is no one who does not come and go, nor ask about long and short; yet they remain fixed before the bedside until the very end, tending to the patient from beginning to finish.

If the merit is already such through the briefest of visits, how much more so for those who, with sincere hearts and genuine intent, protect the life of another in the Western Pure Land through compassion, gentleness, and tireless devotion from start to finish? This is a field of merit.
This is equal to the great void and cannot be described by analogy. Therefore, one should not distinguish between teacher and friend;
once even a single fragment of compassionate concern has been aroused, and as the duty of attending to the sick falls upon you, you should not give rise to resentment or aversion.
Should monastics or laypeople, whether from afar or nearby, come to visit the patient, the person on duty should take the initiative and inform the visitors that they are outside.
"Please be seated. Do not enter the room directly. Why? It is said that there are three reasons for this. First, upon seeing a patient, one must engage in dialogue and discussion;
this does not injure their spirit, yet failing to do so would impair their vital energy (qi). Second, it is out of consideration for worldly propriety.
Second, they send various refreshments such as fruits and teas, and engage in trivial worldly chatter; this either harms their mouths or ruins their stomachs.
Furthermore, they may urge them to summon physicians or consult diviners, seeking deities and taking medicines in all sorts of ways.
It does not merely delude the mind; it immediately disturbs the intention. Since there are these three kinds of harm, it would be better not to see them at all.
To do so is to add further busyness to those who are already capable and to heap more coals upon the sick.

If one asks what benefit there is in this, it is like a wrestling match where one side retreats in defeat while another side comes forward; the host is neither defeated nor diminished, yet he is clearly harmed.
It is so. It is likewise with the sick person: though they do not sink, they are heavy; though they do not die, they perish prematurely—this is also clear.

Therefore, although one may say their intentions are kind, in truth they resemble an enemy. This is because, when it comes to the two characters for "falling ill," one does not distinguish between whether it is difficult or easy to arise.
There is nothing more wondrous than closing the door of the room and silently reciting the Buddha’s name. One must by no means see guests or engage in conversation.

That which ought to be good becomes easily good; even one who is about to die will remain at peace. The nature and consciousness become settled, solitary, and perfect. This is the most wondrous and skillful secret method.
Though it is not extraordinary, you gentlemen may test it for yourselves. Only then can one be called "unworthy" or "a fool among fools."
There is, however, one aperture. Therefore, with the exception of the single person on duty, no others are permitted to enter the door.

Nevertheless, if a great spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) or a pure companion in the practice of nianfo should arrive, you should invite them inside to instruct the patient, so that they may gain strength thereby and proceed directly to the Western Pure Land. Apart from this, none—
In general, one must not enter or exit; for fear that many [distractions] might disturb their spirit, how could one bear such a thing in one's heart?
Thus, when guarding the sick, the person on duty must by no means leave them for even a moment. One should remain close at their side. If they do not ask, [one should still attend to them].
"O, you too should not speak much. It is simply this final causal condition that is fundamentally difficult to resolve.
Therefore, among all things, you must forgive him, show him compassion, look after him, and provide for him.
Just as a minister serves a sovereign or a servant serves a master, you must never give rise to even the slightest thought of resentment; you must ultimately wish for his certain [liberation]."
It is best to see the Buddha when one is born in the Western Pure Land.

However, if their condition gradually worsens day by day and their physical appearance no longer seems right, the caregiver must be even more meticulous in guarding the patient; they should not leave them for even a single step.
This is because at the moment of death, the four elements disintegrate and the eight sufferings torment one simultaneously; even with great strength, it is difficult to avoid the pain. Therefore—

Sitting and lying down are not peaceful; turning over and back brings no rest. Because the tendons, bones, flesh, and blood, along with the network of vessels, all pull simultaneously, it is truly difficult to pass through.
Therefore, one should earnestly allow things to follow their own nature; one must by all means avoid forcing oneself. Let the body fall into sleep of its own accord.

Whether they are lying on their backs, leaning askew, stretching out their legs, or sitting cross-legged—in whatever strange or unusual posture they may be—they must be left as they are and not moved, lest their thoughts be disturbed.
One should instead request others to approach and assist them by chanting the Buddha’s name clearly and audibly.

This is called the foremost sublime Dharma and the foremost grace and virtue. One must by no means raise one's voice or shout loudly, nor act with agitation or haste, for such actions cause harm and panic.
This is because at the moment when life is about to end but has not yet ended, the *hun* and *po* spirits are most subtle and most cold.
This is to prevent harm and to guard against their being startled or terrified. It is like burning incense in a brazier;
if one wishes its smoke to rise straight up to the heavens, it should be kept in quiet stillness without even a speck of dust or a slight breeze to interfere. Only then can it ascend directly upward.
The spirit of a deceased person about to depart is just like this; therefore, during the final moments of death, one should especially employ [these methods].
Mindfully attend to them and slowly recite the Buddha’s name to assist their journey; this is the most essential duty.

One must continue until the deceased’s entire body has grown cold and not a trace of warmth remains. Only then should one conclude the recitation of the Buddha’s name and proceed with the subsequent arrangements.
It is not too late to bathe the body, wash the face, and change the clothes. If the deceased expresses a preference for the coffin, they may be laid in it.
If one is to sit in a joyous niche (*khan*), it is already appropriate; as for lying in a coffin, it truly cannot be discussed. A niche has two meanings: cremation and burial.

Setting aside burial for a moment, let us discuss cremation alone. One must wait until seven days have passed before the fire can be lit (the full details of this are found in the "Account of Departing Westward at the Point of Death").
However, once death has occurred, everything depends upon a capable person acting as the presiding master to protect the dying and the deceased.
These are the attendants; they ought to observe the pure precepts of the Buddha and by no means follow their secular customs. Why is this?

Because while the living cannot be made to conform, the dead must be made to strictly adhere [to the Dharma]. Furthermore, since the living are thus characterized by stinginess and greed that they cannot relinquish, the dead must be made to attain liberation and a state of carefree elegance.
Therefore, whether it be lying in a coffin or sitting in a shrine, whether through cremation or burial, it requires nothing more than [the proper ritual attire].
Two or three garments—enough to cover the upper and lower, the inner and outer—are sufficient, excluding the *kāṣāya*.

If these are placed within a coffin, they may be either winter or summer clothing. However, if one intends to remain seated in a niche and undergo *dhyāpana* (cremation), one must by no means wear cotton.
For the inner and outer, upper and lower, plain linen (*kṣaumaka*) is most excellent; it burns quickly and without odor. Thus it is said.
In my humble view, it is sufficient to have bare feet and a shaven head, appearing as they naturally are in the manner of an Arhat.
Why should one bother to dress up their appearance by donning the red *kaṣāya*, wearing the yellow *haiqing* robe, or putting on the *Guanyin dou* cap?
Are you wearing those Yangzhou shoes? Even if one is a famous monk, or even the abbot of Vairocana Monastery, there is no need for such extreme affectation.
If you say that dressing up here is for the living to see, the deceased are distant and unconscious;
if you say it is for the dead to suffer the torments there, who among the living would ever be willing to take their place?
Therefore, know that the true essence of the Western Paradise lies right before you. Neither in the heavens nor among men do I find joy. Alas!

Since this is so, why do the men and women of the world not diligently practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name? Thus, those who are deluded remain deluded to the end, while those who have awakened are not so.
Furthermore, within this mere bag of stinking skin, there is nothing but a pouch of pus and blood, teeming with ten thousand maggots.
What suffering is it to take the fat and essence of the faithful’s offerings—objects of such rare value—and enclose them within this foul-smelling pus and blood that cannot even be heard?
It is of no benefit whatsoever to the deceased; as for the living, it surely entails transgression. Someone might say:

"The Confucians have the rites of burial and the three sacrifices, and they also maintain the doctrine of shrouds, coffins, and outer cases; these are what ought to be observed. I request [your response].

He explained it, saying: "It is not that I do not practice [the rites], nor that I fail to perform burials and sacrifices; it is not that I do not clothe the deceased or provide coffins and outer cases. Rather, I say this:

while alive one does not rely on the Buddha, yet upon death one ought to follow the Buddhist precepts. Thus, Confucianism and Buddhism appear both similar and distinct. They are similar in principle (*li*), but distinct in ritual law (*fa*).
Since the principles are the same while the laws differ, why must one rely on Confucianism? If one wishes to emulate the Confucians," [he continued].
What need is there to take refuge in Śākyamuni? Having already taken refuge in him, one ought to rely on the Dharma and Vinaya for discussion, rather than using worldly perspectives.
Even if you were his disciple, you would not have been able to bear it had he treated you with such lack of respect.

If you wish to show filial piety by wearing several layers of loose clothing, may you then take those loose garments and all your other clothes and distribute them equally to your fellow practitioners who are dressed in extremely thin and cold attire? Is this not acceptable?
This causes their hearts to rejoice and their minds to be glad, giving rise to a sense of shame, sincerity, and earnestness as they practice pure deeds.

Thus, both teacher and disciple obtain blessings, and both the living and the deceased benefit. How could this not be a case of achieving the beauty of both goals? What a truly joyful matter for us students!

(The Fragrance of Precepts) I am deeply ashamed that my years since leaving home are few and I possess no learning or knowledge. Regarding the four mountains and the places I have passed through, whenever I see each...
Regarding the circumstances of those who shared the same robes, from the time of their passing until their cremation, these matters are often obscured by the mental fabrications of the survivors.
Consequently, the post-mortem traces of the deceased remain no different from those of the worldly laity; this is entirely inappropriate.

One must recognize that such practices not only contravene the Buddha’s regulations but also offer no benefit to the deceased, while instead increasing their karmic faults. This seems truly unbearable to the heart. Deeply...

It is truly lamentable. Therefore, with no other choice, I shall briefly set forth the circumstances—beginning from the onset of this chronic ailment, through until the end of my life, and including the causes and conditions for my protection and care—to speak directly to all you compassionate brothers and sisters throughout the ten directions; may you look upon me with great mercy and compassion.
Pity my lack of talent and allow me to express myself with complete sincerity. I pray that you will not take offense at my crude words or coarse speech, but instead grant me your correction.
I beg that you will permit this to be put into practice, so that both the living and the deceased may receive boundless benefit. Thus, those who tend to the sick and those who provide assistance—
Merit! One shall obtain boundless blessings.

I vow that by means of this expression of my sincere feelings, I shall adorn the Buddha’s Pure Land, universally benefiting all beings to bring peace and happiness to the Land of Universal Peace and Bliss.

I, the mendicant Jixiang, from Yue East and praying for the West, having shed tears of blood, humbly record these words while on a boat at West Lake in Wulin, as I am about to complete my journey westward.
My inner bitterness is difficult to endure;
I have heard that according to the Buddha’s regulations, the cremation of deceased monks was originally intended to cause them to leave behind their illusory bodies of segmented existence.
This is to realize the eternally abiding Dharma-body. Therefore, since ancient times, the monastic communities of all quarters have observed this as a fixed regulation.
However, nowadays, followers of the Śākya school know only to cremate the remains as a way to conclude the matter;

they no longer follow the ancient custom of keeping the coffin in the shrine for several days, claiming that the eight consciousnesses (*vijñānas*) of the deceased have not yet entirely departed and that one still knows their presence.

It is suffering. It is bitter and difficult to express; or rather, it is a resentment so venomous that it is hard to endure. He did not contemplate the suffering of his own rebirth in the many heavens;
he only thought of seeking a seven-day reprieve, considering this to be a most magnificent favor and a supreme virtue—namely, being spared from that extreme, wailing hardship and unbearable agony.
Since this is so, one must necessarily give rise to a compassionate heart of benevolence and practice great...
The skillful means of compassion should be gracious and consoling. May the deceased find peace and receive these offerings; would this not be truly beautiful?
Having traveled to study in various regions, I have often seen those who, within three days or even a single day, proceed to cremate the remains.
This is indeed the height of impropriety. Why? Because although the person has passed away, there is still that which does not perish.
That which remains is precisely the eighth consciousness, the *ālaya-vijñāna*. It merely guards its empty chamber.

This is similar to what Confucius meant by "dying but not perishing. Therefore, in conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it is called the "soul," and in ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it is called the "consciousness-spirit" (*vijñāna-deva*).
For humans are the most spiritual among all things, and this "spirituality" is precisely this consciousness. Thus, one knows that since this consciousness—

If one proceeds immediately to cremate [the body], how could there not be a reason for suffering? Therefore, once suffering arises, there must be resentment harbored within the consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Once resentment is harbored, anger (*dveṣa*) will inevitably arise. Once hatred has arisen, it will certainly cause one to fall into a lower realm.
I ask you: upon whom does the blame for causing such a fall rest? If this is what leads one to fall, where then lies the name of "śramaṇa" and the heart of a "son of the Śākya"?
How would such a person differ from a butcher or a professional executioner?
For this reason, I appeal in sorrow to the elders of the ten directions and all the mountain monasteries: I humbly entreat you to grant the grace of a single thread of compassion.
Compassionately grieving for the suffering of the deceased, one should pause for a minimum of seven days.
According to the supplementary notes on the eight consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), the six consciousnesses—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—depart gradually;

however, these two consciousnesses—the seventh *manas* consciousness and the eighth *ālaya* consciousness—must necessarily remain stagnant until the seventh day before they can finally be completely eliminated. Therefore, it is essential...
It is clear that it is only after allowing [the body] to remain for seven days and cremating it on the eighth day that it will truly benefit the deceased.

During the Xianfeng Xinyou year, while I was residing at Shangfangsi Temple on Mount Tai as a student and reading the various Tripitaka collections, I came across the "Yizi" (Artistry) fascicle, which contains the *Supplementary Notes on the Rules of the Eight Consciousnesses*.
It states: "The Buddha taught that humans possess eight consciousnesses; thus one knows..."
It is consciousness (*vijñāna*). The first five are called eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, and body-consciousness.
The sixth is called mental-consciousness (*manovijñāna*). The seventh is called the manas-consciousness. The eighth is called the *ālaya*-consciousness.

[The other said: "This consciousness is the most spiritual; therefore, it knows pain and itchiness, it knows good and evil. It can respond to all myriad affairs and embodies all manifold principles. It can create both heaven and hell, and it can bring about both sages and the fruit of Buddhahood. In every movement and gesture, there is nothing that is not it."
[It] arises. If that [consciousness] were not present, it would be called a "dead thing.
Among humans, when born, this eighth consciousness is the very first to arrive; the seven consciousnesses, the sixth consciousness, and the five consciousnesses follow.
They arrive one after another in succession. When death occurs, it is this eighth consciousness alone that departs last;

the five consciousnesses, the sixth consciousness, and the seventh consciousness all depart beforehand. Indeed, the eighth consciousness is the spiritual consciousness of a person, what the world commonly calls the "soul.
Since this consciousness is spiritual, at the very moment a person first conceives in the womb, it arrives first.
It comes; it is precisely because it comes first that while the child is in the mother’s womb, it is an active entity.
When a person dies and the breath has ceased, the spirit does not depart immediately, but must wait until the entire body has become cold and there is not a single trace of warmth remaining.

That consciousness is just about to depart. Once consciousness has departed, this body appears to be entirely devoid of awareness. [I said: "Even though it is entirely devoid of awareness, one should regard it as if it were still alive and cherish it.

One should guard it carefully and slowly recite the Buddha’s name, so that by means of the power of the Buddha’s six-eight vows, it may be like darkness meeting a lamp, the sea of suffering meeting a boat, or one who has lost their way meeting a guide.

Lead it forward slowly, causing its spirit to become courageous and its mind peaceful, so that it may see the Buddha with composure. Therefore, if there is even one spot that is slightly warm, then the eighth consciousness has not yet departed.
The [suffering] has not yet been completely eliminated. Because it has not been completely eliminated, one still experiences pain.

Since one still experiences pain, not only is the agony of cremation beyond description, but even the forced exertion of moving the body or sitting in the cross-legged posture remains difficult to endure.
It is simply that the body cannot move, the mouth cannot speak, and the mind cannot manifest itself. How tragic! (I said:

One must understand that to have a mouth yet be unable to speak is like a mute being subjected to physical execution, or an infant encountering fire and water. Having raised one's eyes only to find no kin, to possess a mouth yet be unable to express oneself is the most tragic of all tragedies.

It is essential to rest, offer solace, and share in their grief; compassion is what is required. The *Classic of Filial Piety* says: "Vitality (*āyuḥ*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—these three are never separated from one another. Indeed.
It is said that as long as the human body possesses warmth, it possesses consciousness; and as long as it possesses consciousness, its lifespan is not yet exhausted.

Therefore, throughout antiquity, there have been many instances where those who had died for three or five days were restored to life; these are all fully recorded in the canonical texts and can be verified with clarity.

(If this is the case, how can one simply cremate a person immediately upon death? Even if they were able to return to life, their room would already have been destroyed—where could they go to find lodging? Furthermore, how could the resentment harbored by the deceased and the karmic consequences for the living be resolved?)
Examining the Confucian tradition, there is likewise the rite of the "great encoffining" on the third day.

This is based on the affection of one's kinsmen, who still hold out hope that [the deceased] might perhaps return to life. For us who have come to the monastic order, it is originally a matter of acting in accordance with the natural course of things;
although we do not harbor deluded hopes for their return to life, how could we fail to empathize with the circumstances of their suffering? And yet—
"Why did you so hastily set fire to it? Where, then, is your heart of compassion and skillful means?

Alas! We see that even when a rabbit dies, a fox grieves; each feels sorrow for its own kind. If things are thus among animals, how much more so should it be among those who share the same human nature, and especially among those who share the same monastic lineage?
Furthermore, when human suffering reaches its most extreme point, a mind of anger arises with the utmost ease."
Because of a mind of anger, one causes oneself to fall into ruin. One must understand that as for the transgression of causing another to fall, to whom does that fault belong?
(One should treat them with compassion and pity; I entreat you, O Benevolent One, to bestow the grace of skillful means. After seven days, burn [the body] again. The Sūtra says:
King Ajātaśatru established a stūpa and temple for the Buddha; his merit was most magnificent. When he approached the end of his life, his attendants held...
A fan fell by mistake onto the King’s face. The King gave rise to a single thought of anger and, after death, immediately took the body of a snake.
Later, he encountered a śramaṇa, heard the sutras and the Dharma, and was thereby able to be reborn in heaven.

Observing this, one can know that as long as the consciousness of the deceased has not entirely departed, it is truly unbearable and truly improper to cremate them. Why? Because it causes them to suffer due to that pain.
To give rise to anger and cause harm that leads others to fall into ruin is the most cruel of all cruelties. Let me ask:

what enmity do I have with the deceased, and what cause for resentment? To perform such an evil deed under the guise of a "good intention," thereby causing them to swallow their bitterness and harbor hatred, is truly beyond the bounds of human endurance.
Some may say that the matter is remote and vague, leaving no way to...
Those who investigate should joyfully consult the Buddhist scriptures; they are recorded therein with great clarity.
One must understand that if the words of the Buddha are not believed, what words can be trusted? Why, then, should one assume the title of śramaṇa or bhikṣu to become a disciple of the Buddha-gate?
Generally, the living do not pity the suffering of the deceased, while those who act as hosts fear that the duration [of the funeral rites] will be prolonged.
It is wasteful; or rather, because other matters are so numerous, one seeks only to expedite the process and merely settle the formalities.
Consequently, there is no careful attention or meticulous observation, nor is there any consideration of whether the deceased is comfortable or distressed.
This has become the norm, such that even when someone mentions this matter or discusses these principles, others instead laugh it off as pedantic. This causes the deceased to suffer.
It is difficult to extend [the legs]. Alas, how lamentable! Generally, among the three teachings of Confucianism, Buddhism, and Taoism, this matter ought to be treated with compassion.

Among those who have left the household life, there may be cases where the body has become cold and the legs stiff, making it difficult to position them for sitting. However, there is a method to treat this:
one need only use hot water to wash and rinse [the legs], and then apply a cloth soaked in hot water over the knees of the deceased; thus, the knees—
Generally speaking, one's own ability can be softened so that it remains flexible enough to coil. Even if one cannot coil it, it can still be secured with a strap.
Furthermore, the practice of meditation and the two words "rebirth in the Western Paradise" certainly do not depend upon the legs.
Why then do you insist on practicing with such formality, seeking speed while completely disregarding the suffering involved? This is the case with my disciple Jie Xiang.
I crawl on my belly across the ten directions, entreating all you great benevolent elders and the abbots of various monasteries:
please grant the favor of your skillful means and, out of compassion, suspend the cremation for seven days. This would serve as a supreme merit and establish our final virtuous connection.
Will you not deign to take pity upon him and graciously grant my request? You must know that as long as one has not yet transcended the three realms, this suffering persists.
It is difficult for anyone to escape this; those said to be able to form karmic conditions with them are, in fact, forming karmic conditions with me.
Since we both harbor such intentions and extend such compassion, when the time of death arrives, the Buddha will surely take pity on us and accept us.
Furthermore, the benevolent ones of all quarters will also surely employ skillful means for our sake. Therefore, if...
If one person can practice it, then perhaps hundreds of people will practice it. If ten people practice it, then perhaps thousands of people will practice it.
If hundreds of thousands, millions, billions, or tens of billions of people practice it, then all the people throughout the ten directions and pervading the entire Dharma-realm will do so.
Furthermore, there is none who does not delight in virtuous conduct. May all the deceased monks throughout the empire be bathed in this great grace and entirely transcend into the pure realm.
Are they not, indeed, like parents who have given them a second birth, or like teachers and masters encountered once more?

For this reason, I, Jie Xiang, most piteously appeal to the benevolent ones of all quarters, as well as those currently holding authority, leaders, and administrators, earnestly entreating you to practice great compassion.
With compassion, you have opened the way through great skillful means, each with loving and sincere grace toward the seven heavens.
I, your disciple, throughout life after life, shall never forget this original intention nor fail to repay this debt of gratitude.
Even if I should fall into the various realms of existence, I vow to offer my service and never forget the kindness of your rebirth-giving grace. I humbly entreat you.
Venerable Elders of all quarters, I humbly request your universal favor.
With the utmost earnestness and fervent supplication, I address you once more: What is the ultimate suffering and most tragic state in this world?
None is greater than the moment when life is at its end. Reflecting calmly upon the interval between being alive and about to die, it is like a living tortoise being stripped of its shell.
Like a live crab cast into boiling water, the four great elements disintegrate all at once, and the eight sufferings simultaneously sear one’s being.
This state of agonizing distress is truly beyond the reach of a single word; it is difficult to describe even with a mouth. I ask:

who is able to empathize with this bitterness, perceive this suffering, and know this pain? To rescue one from such hardship—how difficult that would be! Even if one possessed the utmost filial piety...
One's descendants, worthy disciples, and virtuous friends likewise cannot replace them. Alas! Although they cannot replace them, there is indeed a most wondrous and singular means of succor:
if even a hair’s breadth of warmth remains in the deceased’s corpse, then the master of the house has certainly not yet departed.
Since the master has not yet departed, one must allow him to rely upon it; whether sitting, leaning, lying on the back, or sleeping on the side.
Whether stretching or contracting, hanging the feet, or sitting cross-legged—manifesting various postures—one must allow them to occur naturally;
by no means should one force or adjust them. Why? Because this very moment is truly a critical juncture of life and death.
Since one cannot seek birth and yet it is not obtained, nor can one seek death and yet it is not obtained, it is exactly like a living bird.

They are steamed while still alive in bamboo cages; living creatures are subjected to the torment of flames. The reality of their plight is most cruel, and the extent of their suffering is beyond words.
Therefore, one should watch over them with great care; only after they have completely cooled may they be prepared for consumption.
According to the Brahmajāla Sūtra, tending to the sick is already considered the foremost field of merit; how much more so this [case].
As for the matter at hand: even if it be a scorching day, one should pause for a short while to ensure everything is properly arranged.
Then, whether placing [the remains] in an open field or within a kiln, wait until the morning of the eighth day before performing the cremation once again.
Yet, witnessing such a heart-wrenching scene with one's own eyes, it recalls what Mencius said:
"I would rather see them alive than bear to see them die. Since one cannot bear to see them die, one should especially feel compassion and pity for them;

the most effective way to do so is to focus one's mind entirely on assisting them in reciting the Buddha’s name. Whether the number of people is many or few, what matters is that they be close by the bedside.
First, set out a single incense burner. It may contain a Buddha image, or it may be without one; either is acceptable.
You need only use a hand chime and small bells, reciting "Namo Amitābha Buddha" slowly. The sound must not be too loud, for fear of startling the deceased's consciousness;
you must recite with a peaceful and even tone, so as to cause the deceased’s mind to be at ease and their spirit to be stable. As for their transgressions...
They encountered a pardon and crossed over by encountering a boat; they were exceedingly joyful.

Even if one has committed the five sins of immediate retribution or suffers great agony, according to the *Kṣitigarbha Sūtra*, when such a person is at the point of death, if others recite the Buddha’s name for them, their offenses will gradually be extinguished even within that state of suffering. Why is this? It is because they rely upon the vows of the Buddha.
Power, as well as the power of mindfulness supported by the multitude—just as when a sinner has already approached the presence of a king, the weak find their powerful protector;
how could they not be freed from suffering and hardship, and reach pure tranquility?

If it is thus, is this not the formation of a most excellent and auspicious condition, and assistance toward a most magnificent virtuous deed? Furthermore, as it is said in the *Lun* (Treatise): "In daily practice..."
For those who are virtuous, the heat rises from below to above; for those who commit evil, it descends from above to below.

If the heat pervades the entire body and returns to the crown of the head, this is the path of the sages (*ārya*). If it reaches the eyes, it is the path of the gods (*deva*). If it reaches the heart, it is the path of humans (*manuṣya*).
If it reaches the abdomen, it is the path of hungry ghosts (*preta*). If it reaches the knees, it is the path of animals (*tiryagyoni*). If it reaches the soles of the feet, [it is the path of hell].
As for "those who emerge," this refers to the hell realm. A verse states:
"The crown of the head is for the sages, the eyes for those born as devas; The human heart, the belly for hungry ghosts;
The knees for animals, and from the soles of the feet one emerges into hell."
Alas! As for these two characters, "birth" and "death," who among people can escape them? The Sūtra says:
"Even if you have practiced goodness throughout your entire life, if at the moment of death you give rise to a single evil thought, you will immediately fall into the evil realms.

Conversely, if you have committed evil throughout your life but later are able to repent and cultivate a virtuous mind, and if at the moment of death you are once again able to recite the Buddha’s name, you will be reborn in the good paths. Alas! This is the final word.
This "Gate" (Kuan) is truly the most critical and most vital matter.

Therefore, regardless of whether one is a monk or a layperson, noble or humble, throughout one’s life as a human being, this single moment is of paramount importance. How could one afford to be negligent and thereby harm oneself, leading to a fall?
Is this not tragic? Is it not imperative to be cautious?
When one suffers from illness and loathing, being defiled by excrement and urine and the body becoming impure, one does not dare to recite the Buddha’s name.

Indeed, the fruit of *buddhānusmṛti* (recollection of the Buddha) depends upon purity; therefore, while free from illness and worldly affairs, it is precisely appropriate to practice *buddhānusmṛti* early on and to prepare one's own provisions for the path.
If one should fall gravely ill, with excrement and urine upon one's bed, one will realize the impurity of the body.
The practitioner fears committing transgressions and thus does not dare to recite; yet in guarding against them, there is further suffering, and being unable to maintain mastery, they cannot recite.
Alas! They fail to realize that when a great illness approaches death, it is just like rowing a boat upstream against the current:
one must strive with all one's might to push the oars and pull the ropes to achieve success. Once one reaches the headwaters, if the oars are even slightly...
Stop! If the hawser slackens even slightly, the boat will surely capsize. Therefore, in the moment between life and death, it is entirely vital to recite the Buddha’s name with single-minded focus.
Let it be—regardless of urine, excrement, filth, or the impurity of your entire body.
You need only not fear death; you must exert yourself and be willing to recite. Next, when I reach Zhang and he dies, I shall strive to the utmost and risk my very life.

Set your mind on reciting. Cease worrying about whether he lives or dies. Clench your teeth with determination and continue reciting with all your might until your breath seems as if it has been severed;

only then may you stop. If you do not recite because you fear impurity, or because of pain, or because of grief, or because you lack the strength to manage your sorrow, or because there is no one present to take your place— [This is a fragmentary excerpt from a liturgical or meditative instruction concerning the practice of *nien-fo* (recitation of the Buddha's name) during the terminal illness of another.]

If one does not even think of the bitter, and so on, up to not thinking of deluded thoughts, not thinking of greedy attachment, not thinking of emotional affection, and not thinking due to being stupefied and ignorant—would this not be a life wasted?
Would it not be a mere pretense of wearing the black robes and a hollow attempt at being human?
Furthermore, if one recites as if not reciting, lacking any sincere faith, aspiration, or earnestness, remaining merely indifferent—even if one recites to the point of...

Even if Maitreya descends to earth, it will still be difficult to be reborn there; therefore, one must maintain precise faith and aspiration during one’s daily life and apply oneself with even greater earnestness at the time of death.
This is as swift as a fine steed leaving its stable or a sail being unfurled with a following current.

Next, one should have both faith and aspiration earnest during the day, and at the moment of death, further request a spiritual teacher (*kalyāṇamitra*) to assist them in reciting the Buddha’s name, ensuring that the sound of the Buddha enters their ears.
Even if suffering arises, you must not dwell upon it yourself; rather, you should recognize it as an aid for my practice of *nien-fo*, causing my own nature to enter into the Buddha-name.
May the Buddha’s radiance guide and draw forth my spirit.

Although rebirth while still carrying one's karma is indeed difficult to attain, you must by all means avoid being terrified by filth and pollution, lest you dare not recite the Buddha’s name. Why? Because the Buddha...

He is called the Greatly Compassionate and Greatly Merciful One; there is certainly no principle by which he would not provide salvation. For example, when the sun of midday hangs in the sky, how could it distinguish between high and low, noble and base?
When the ocean receives the hundred rivers, how could it deliberate upon what is pure or defiled? Yet the Buddha neither suffers nor extracts [suffering].
There is no hardship that will not be rescued; one need only fear that your faith and aspiration are not earnest, and that your mind is further inverted—then your suffering would be beyond words.
If your faith, aspiration, and practice are all earnest, and you are able to maintain clear right mindfulness at the moment of death, then you will certainly be reborn in accordance with your vow.
Were it otherwise, the Buddhas and Amitābha Buddha would be speaking falsehoods. Consider this carefully.
Is there not such a principle? Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says, "All things are created solely by the mind.
I only wish that you would develop such deep faith, vowing to practice with earnest resolve. Anything other than this is called frivolous conceptualization.

If these words of mine are not spoken with the sincerity of one who would rather have his heart torn out, may my fragrance of precepts never again reach my tongue for all eternity. You should believe this deeply.
Practice this with diligence.
